topics.title: What accounting is, who uses it and why
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Define accounting and distinguish it from book-keeping
  • Name the main users of financial statements and what each one wants to know
  • Distinguish financial, cost and management accounting

About 45 minutes

Definition

Accounting. The process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating the financial transactions of an organisation so that users can take informed decisions.

Book-keeping is the clerical part: noting every transaction in the right book. Accounting begins where book-keeping stops. It classifies those entries, summarises them into statements, and interprets the result. A shop assistant who enters bills in a register is book-keeping. The person who tells the owner that credit sales are growing faster than collections is accounting.

Why bother? Because memory fails and owners cheat themselves. Without records you cannot say how much profit the business made, how much customers owe you, how much you owe suppliers, or whether the bank loan can be repaid. Law also requires it: the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company to keep proper books of account, and the Income-tax Act and GST law require records from any business above their thresholds.

Who uses accounting information
UserTypical questionWhat they look at
Owner or proprietorDid I earn a profit and can I withdraw money?Profit and loss account, drawings, capital
Lender or bankCan this business repay my loan with interest?Cash flow, current ratio, debt-equity ratio
SupplierWill I be paid on credit terms?Current liabilities, payment record, liquidity
InvestorIs the business growing and is it worth its price?Earnings, return on equity, trends
EmployeesCan the firm afford wage increases and is my job safe?Profitability and stability
Government and tax authoritiesIs tax computed correctly on the true income?Books for income tax and GST returns
Customers and the publicWill this firm still exist to honour warranties?Financial strength, solvency

Accounting has three main branches. Financial accounting records historical transactions and reports to outsiders through standard statements. Cost accounting works out what each product or service costs to make. Management accounting uses both to help managers plan and control. This course is about financial accounting; the other two build on it in later semesters.

In India

A kirana store and a listed company use the same double-entry logic. What differs is the rulebook: a sole proprietor mainly follows the Income-tax Act and the GST Acts, while a company must follow the Companies Act, 2013 and the accounting standards notified under it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which of the following is a function of accounting rather than book-keeping?
  • Preparing the balance sheet and interpreting it (correct)
  • Entering a sale in the sales register
  • Filing vouchers in date order
  • Posting a journal entry to the ledger

Summarising and interpreting are accounting functions. Recording and posting are book-keeping.

2. A bank deciding whether to grant a loan is mainly interested in the business's
  • Advertising budget
  • Ability to repay (correct)
  • Brand name
  • Number of branches

Lenders look at repayment capacity: cash flows, liquidity and solvency.

Common mistakes

  • Treating accounting as only a tax chore. Its first customer is the owner.
  • Writing 'accounting is the language of business' with no explanation. Say what it communicates and to whom.
Exam tip

For a 5-mark definition question write the definition, name the stages (identify, measure, record, classify, summarise, communicate) and add one line on users. Three parts get full marks.

Try it yourself: Distinguish between book-keeping and accounting. Give one example of each.

Model answer. Book-keeping is the systematic recording of transactions, for example entering a credit sale in the sales book. Accounting includes classifying and summarising those records and interpreting the results, for example preparing the profit and loss account and explaining why profit fell. Book-keeping is routine and clerical; accounting needs judgement and produces information for decisions.

topics.title: Accounting concepts, conventions and the standards framework
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • State and apply the basic accounting concepts and conventions
  • Explain why accounting rules are standardised
  • Outline the Indian framework: Accounting Standards (AS), Ind AS, ICAI, MCA and NFRA

About 60 minutes

If every accountant were free to measure things differently, two businesses could not be compared and no lender would trust a balance sheet. The profession therefore works to a shared set of rules called Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, or GAAP. In India GAAP means the Companies Act, 2013, the accounting standards notified under it, and accepted accounting practice.

Basic accounting concepts
ConceptWhat it saysQuick example
Business entityThe business is separate from its ownerRohan's personal grocery bill is not a business expense
Money measurementOnly transactions measurable in money are recordedThe skill of a manager is not an asset in the books
Going concernThe business will continue for the foreseeable futureMachinery is valued at cost less depreciation, not at scrap value
Accounting periodProfit is reported for a fixed period, usually a yearIndian businesses use 1 April to 31 March
CostAssets are recorded at purchase costLand bought for 20 lakh stays at 20 lakh even if it is now worth 50 lakh
Dual aspectEvery transaction has two equal effectsBuying furniture for cash raises furniture and lowers cash
RealisationRevenue is recognised when it is earned, not when advance is receivedAn order is not a sale until goods are delivered
AccrualRecord income and expense when they arise, not when cash movesMarch rent paid in April belongs to March
MatchingCharge the expenses of a period against the revenue of that same periodCost of goods sold sits in the same year as the sale
Accounting conventions
ConventionMeaning
ConsistencyUse the same methods year after year so results can be compared
Conservatism (prudence)Provide for all expected losses, do not anticipate profits
MaterialityRecord items that could change a decision; ignore trivial ones
Full disclosureStatements must reveal everything that a user needs to know

Accounting standards turn these ideas into detailed rules. In India they are issued in two layers. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) recommends standards; the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) notifies them under the Companies Act. Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards) are converged with IFRS and apply to listed companies and to unlisted companies with net worth of 250 crore rupees or more, along with their holding, subsidiary and associate companies. Smaller companies follow the older Accounting Standards (AS). The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) oversees the quality of audit and compliance for larger companies.

Watch out

A sole proprietor is not bound by the Companies Act, but the concepts above still apply, and the Income-tax Act expects the books to follow a consistent method of accounting.

Tip

Conservatism is the concept students misuse most. It means do not overstate profit or assets. It does not mean deliberately hide profit; hidden reserves are a violation of true and fair presentation.

Key terms: concepts and standards

Accounting period
The span for which accounts are prepared, usually 12 months; in India commonly 1 April to 31 March.
Accrual
Recording income and expenses when earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid.
GAAP
Generally accepted accounting principles, the shared rules of accounting.
Ind AS
Indian Accounting Standards, converged with IFRS and applicable to companies meeting notified thresholds.
Asset
A resource owned by the business from which future benefit is expected.
Liability
An obligation of the business to pay money or give value to outsiders.
Contingent liability
A possible obligation that depends on a future event, such as a discounted bill being dishonoured.

Check what you just learned

1. Purchase of a machine for 5,00,000 is recorded at that amount even if its market value rises to 7,00,000 next year. Which concept applies?
  • Going concern
  • Realisation
  • Materiality
  • Cost concept (correct)

Assets are recorded at cost; later market rises are not recognised.

2. Providing for doubtful debts but not recording expected extra profit reflects
  • Consistency
  • Entity
  • Conservatism (correct)
  • Materiality

Expected losses are provided for, anticipated profits are not recorded.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up accrual with cash basis. Accrual follows the event; cash follows the money.
  • Saying Ind AS apply to all companies. They apply only to those meeting the notified thresholds.
Exam tip

When asked to 'explain with example', give the concept in one line and a rupee example in the next. Examiners award the example.

Try it yourself: Why do accounting standards exist? Name the Indian bodies involved.

Model answer. Standards make financial statements comparable and reliable by prescribing common measurement and disclosure rules. In India the ICAI formulates and recommends standards, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs notifies them under the Companies Act, 2013, and NFRA monitors audit and compliance quality for larger companies. Ind AS, converged with IFRS, apply to listed companies and unlisted companies with net worth of 250 crore rupees or more; others follow AS.

topics.title: The accounting equation and how transactions change it
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • State the accounting equation and its two forms
  • Analyse a transaction by its effect on assets, liabilities and capital
  • Show that the equation holds after every transaction

About 50 minutes

Formula · Accounting equation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital

Capital is what the owner has put in plus profits retained, minus drawings. It is also called owner's equity.

Everything the business owns (assets) is funded either by outsiders (liabilities) or by the owner (capital). That is why both sides always match. The equation is the reason double entry works: if a transaction touches one side, something else must change to keep the balance.

Transactions fall into a handful of patterns. Some swap one asset for another (cash for furniture). Some raise an asset and a liability together (goods on credit). Some raise an asset and capital (owner invests cash, or a sale earns a profit). Some reduce an asset and capital together (rent paid, drawings). Whatever the pattern, total assets remain equal to liabilities plus capital.

Tip

A profit does not arrive in a separate box. Selling goods that cost 60,000 for 90,000 raises assets by 30,000 net, and capital by the same 30,000. Profit is simply an increase in capital from operations.

Worked example

Six transactions of Rohan Stationers

Rohan starts a stationery shop and these things happen in the first month: (1) Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash as capital. (2) Buys furniture for 80,000 cash. (3) Buys goods worth 1,50,000 on credit from Sharma Traders. (4) Sells goods that cost 60,000 for 90,000 cash. (5) Pays shop rent 20,000 in cash. (6) Pays Sharma Traders 1,00,000. Show the position after each transaction.

  1. After (1): Cash 5,00,000 = Capital 5,00,000.
  2. After (2): Cash 4,20,000 + Furniture 80,000 = 5,00,000. One asset swapped for another.
  3. After (3): Cash 4,20,000 + Furniture 80,000 + Stock 1,50,000 = 6,50,000. Creditors 1,50,000 + Capital 5,00,000 = 6,50,000.
  4. After (4): Cash 5,10,000 + Furniture 80,000 + Stock 90,000 = 6,80,000. Capital rises by the profit of 30,000 to 5,30,000. Creditors 1,50,000 + Capital 5,30,000 = 6,80,000.
  5. After (5): Cash falls to 4,90,000 and capital falls by the rent to 5,10,000. Assets 6,60,000 = Creditors 1,50,000 + Capital 5,10,000.
  6. After (6): Cash 3,90,000 + Furniture 80,000 + Stock 90,000 = 5,60,000. Creditors 50,000 + Capital 5,10,000 = 5,60,000.

Answer. Final position: Assets 5,60,000 = Creditors 50,000 + Capital 5,10,000.

Watch the accounting equation hold, transaction by transaction

  1. Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash to start the stationery shop. Cash comes in, and the owner's claim on the business grows by the same amount.
  2. He buys furniture for 80,000 and pays cash. One asset swaps for another, so total assets do not move.
  3. He buys goods worth 1,50,000 on credit from Sharma Traders. Assets and a liability both rise by 1,50,000. Nothing has been paid yet.
  4. He sells goods that cost 60,000 for 90,000 cash. Cash rises by 90,000 and stock falls by 60,000, so assets gain 30,000. That profit belongs to the owner, so capital rises by 30,000.
  5. He pays shop rent of 20,000 in cash. An expense uses up cash and reduces what the owner is entitled to, so assets and capital both fall.
  6. He pays Sharma Traders 1,00,000. Cash and the amount owed both fall by 1,00,000.

Check what you just learned

1. If total assets are 8,00,000 and liabilities are 3,00,000, capital is
  • 11,00,000
  • 5,00,000 (correct)
  • 3,00,000
  • 8,00,000

Capital = Assets minus Liabilities = 8,00,000 - 3,00,000.

2. Purchasing goods on credit
  • Raises assets and liabilities (correct)
  • Raises assets and capital
  • Lowers assets and liabilities
  • Changes only liabilities

Stock (asset) and creditors (liability) both rise.

Common mistakes

  • Recording the full sale price as profit. Profit is selling price less cost.
  • Forgetting that drawings and expenses reduce capital.
Exam tip

In a transaction table, always write the new total of both sides after each line. If they differ, you have an error to find before moving on.

Try it yourself: Mohan started a business with cash 2,00,000. He bought goods for 50,000 cash and sold half of them for 40,000 cash. State the assets and capital at the end.

Model answer. Cash after purchase 1,50,000; goods 50,000. Goods sold cost 25,000 for 40,000 so profit 15,000. Cash 1,90,000 + goods 25,000 = assets 2,15,000. Capital 2,00,000 + profit 15,000 = 2,15,000.
keyPoints: Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital

topics.title: Double entry, types of accounts and the accounting cycle
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain the double-entry principle
  • Classify accounts and apply the rules of debit and credit
  • Outline the accounting cycle from voucher to financial statements

About 55 minutes

Double entry means each transaction is recorded twice: once as a debit in one account and once as a credit of an equal amount in another. Debit simply means the left side of an account and credit the right side. The words carry no moral meaning. They are a convention that lets the whole set of books be checked by a single test: total debits must equal total credits.

Modern classification and rules of debit and credit
Type of accountExamplesDebit whenCredit when
AssetCash, stock, furniture, debtors, bankIt increasesIt decreases
LiabilityCreditors, bank loan, outstanding expensesIt decreasesIt increases
Capital (owner's equity)Capital, reservesIt decreases (drawings)It increases
Expense or lossRent, salaries, discount allowedIt increasesIt decreases
Income or gainSales, commission received, interest receivedIt decreasesIt increases

The traditional classification groups accounts as personal (people and firms: Sunil's account, bank account), real (assets and goods: cash, furniture) and nominal (income and expenses: rent, sales). Its rules are: debit the receiver and credit the giver for personal accounts; debit what comes in and credit what goes out for real accounts; debit all expenses and losses and credit all incomes and gains for nominal accounts. Both systems give the same answers. The modern approach is easier to carry into company accounts, so use it as your default and keep the traditional rules for exam questions that ask for them.

The accounting cycle

  1. Collect source documents: invoices, bills, vouchers, bank statements
  2. Journalise: record each transaction in the journal or a subsidiary book
  3. Post to the ledger and balance each account
  4. Prepare the unadjusted trial balance
  5. Pass adjusting entries for items such as depreciation, outstanding and prepaid expenses
  6. Prepare the adjusted trial balance
  7. Prepare the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet
  8. Pass closing entries and open the next period with the closing balances
Watch out

A debit balance is not 'bad' and a credit balance is not 'good'. Cash with a debit balance is healthy. A bank with a credit balance means you are overdrawn.

Worked example

Applying the rules to six transactions

Identify the accounts affected and which side to debit and credit: (a) Started business with cash 1,00,000. (b) Bought furniture for 30,000 by cash. (c) Purchased goods from Anil on credit 40,000. (d) Sold goods for cash 25,000. (e) Paid salaries 8,000. (f) Received commission 5,000.

  1. (a) Cash (asset up) Dr 1,00,000; Capital (capital up) Cr 1,00,000.
  2. (b) Furniture (asset up) Dr 30,000; Cash (asset down) Cr 30,000.
  3. (c) Purchases (expense of trading, up) Dr 40,000; Anil (liability up) Cr 40,000.
  4. (d) Cash (asset up) Dr 25,000; Sales (income up) Cr 25,000.
  5. (e) Salaries (expense up) Dr 8,000; Cash (asset down) Cr 8,000.
  6. (f) Cash (asset up) Dr 5,000; Commission received (income up) Cr 5,000.
Journal entries
EntryDebitAmountCreditAmount
aCash A/c Dr1,00,000To Capital A/c1,00,000
bFurniture A/c Dr30,000To Cash A/c30,000
cPurchases A/c Dr40,000To Anil A/c40,000
dCash A/c Dr25,000To Sales A/c25,000
eSalaries A/c Dr8,000To Cash A/c8,000
fCash A/c Dr5,000To Commission received A/c5,000

Answer. Total debits = total credits = 2,08,000 across the six entries.

Check what you just learned

1. Which account is debited when rent is paid?
  • Rent (correct)
  • Cash
  • Capital
  • Landlord

Rent is an expense, which is debited when it increases. Cash is credited.

2. An increase in a liability is recorded by
  • Credit (correct)
  • Debit
  • Either
  • Neither

Liabilities increase on the credit side.

Common mistakes

  • Debiting the giver in a personal account. Think who received the benefit.
  • Treating drawings as an expense. It is a reduction of capital and is not in the profit and loss account.
Exam tip

Before writing any entry, say the two accounts aloud: 'which two accounts, which is asset, liability, capital, expense or income, up or down?' The side follows automatically.

Try it yourself: State the golden rules of accounting under the traditional approach.

Model answer. Personal account: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

practical.title: Case study: The tea stall that could not say if it made money
practical.intro: Savita runs a tea stall near a metro station in Delhi. She started 18 months ago with 40,000 of her own savings and 30,000 borrowed from a relative. She keeps her daily sales in a pocket diary, pays suppliers in cash, and uses the same cash box for stall money and household expenses. Last week a microfinance lender asked for her profit figure. She cannot give one.
steps:
Which accounting concept is Savita breaking when she uses the same cash box for stall and household expenses? Explain the consequence.
Check your thinking
  • Business entity concept
  • Personal spending mixes with business, so profit is understated or overstated and the lender cannot trust any figure
  • Fix: separate cash box or bank account and record drawings explicitly

Write the accounting equation for her business on the day she started.
Check your thinking
  • Assets (cash) 70,000 = Liabilities (loan) 30,000 + Capital 40,000

Name the minimum set of records she should start to maintain and the reason for each.
Check your thinking
  • Cash book for receipts and payments
  • A simple sales register or daily summary for revenue
  • A purchases and expenses record for matching cost to income
  • A drawings register so household use is not treated as stall expense

topics.title: Journal and ledger
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Pass journal entries with proper narration, including compound entries
  • Post journal entries to ledger accounts
  • Balance a ledger account and carry the balance down

About 60 minutes

The journal is the book of original entry. A transaction is first written there in date order, with the account to be debited, the account to be credited, the amount, and a short narration explaining it. Nothing is lost between a voucher and the books if every entry is made in the journal first.

Format of a journal entry
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (Rs)Credit (Rs)
2026-04-01Cash A/c ......... Dr.3,00,000
To Capital A/c3,00,000
(Being business started with cash)

A compound entry combines several debits or credits in one entry when they arise from one transaction, for example buying goods partly for cash and partly on credit. The only requirement is that total debits equal total credits.

The ledger is the book of final entry: a separate account for every person, asset, liability, income and expense. Posting means copying each journal line to the account named in it, on the same side. Once all postings are made, each account is totalled and balanced. The balance is the difference between the two sides, carried down to open the next period. A debit balance on an asset account means it is a resource of the business; a credit balance on a creditor account means money is owed.

Tip

In the ledger the 'To' and 'By' prefixes only point to the other account. Write the name of the other account on every line so that you can trace the entry in both books.

Worked example

Journal and cash account for Rohan Stationers, April 2026

Journalise and post the cash account: 1 Apr started business with cash 3,00,000; 2 Apr bought goods for cash 80,000; 5 Apr bought goods from Verma & Co on credit 60,000; 8 Apr sold goods for cash 50,000; 10 Apr sold goods to Gupta on credit 40,000; 15 Apr paid rent 10,000; 20 Apr received 25,000 from Gupta; 25 Apr paid 30,000 to Verma & Co.

  1. 1 Apr: Cash Dr 3,00,000 / To Capital 3,00,000.
  2. 2 Apr: Purchases Dr 80,000 / To Cash 80,000.
  3. 5 Apr: Purchases Dr 60,000 / To Verma & Co 60,000.
  4. 8 Apr: Cash Dr 50,000 / To Sales 50,000.
  5. 10 Apr: Gupta Dr 40,000 / To Sales 40,000.
  6. 15 Apr: Rent Dr 10,000 / To Cash 10,000.
  7. 20 Apr: Cash Dr 25,000 / To Gupta 25,000.
  8. 25 Apr: Verma & Co Dr 30,000 / To Cash 30,000.
  9. Cash account debit side: 3,00,000 + 50,000 + 25,000 = 3,75,000. Credit side: 80,000 + 10,000 + 30,000 = 1,20,000. Balance c/d = 2,55,000 (debit).
Journal entries
EntryDebitAmountCreditAmount
1 AprCash A/c Dr3,00,000To Capital A/c3,00,000
2 AprPurchases A/c Dr80,000To Cash A/c80,000
5 AprPurchases A/c Dr60,000To Verma & Co A/c60,000
8 AprCash A/c Dr50,000To Sales A/c50,000
10 AprGupta A/c Dr40,000To Sales A/c40,000

25 AprVerma & Co A/c Dr30,000To Cash A/c30,000

Answer. Cash balance 2,55,000 Dr; Gupta owes 15,000; Rohan owes Verma & Co 30,000.

Journalise Rohan's first six transactions

Pick the account to debit and the account to credit for each transaction. Your ledger and trial balance build up as you post.

  1. Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash as capital.
    Dr Cash ₹5,00,000; Cr Capital ₹5,00,000. Cash is an asset that increased, so debit it. Capital is what the business owes the owner and it increased, so credit it.
  2. Bought furniture for 80,000 and paid cash.
    Dr Furniture ₹80,000; Cr Cash ₹80,000. Furniture (an asset) comes in, so debit it. Cash (an asset) goes out, so credit it.
  3. Bought goods for 1,50,000 on credit from Sharma Traders.
    Dr Purchases ₹1,50,000; Cr Sharma Traders ₹1,50,000. Purchases is an expense-type account that increased, so debit it. Sharma Traders is now owed money, a liability that increased, so credit it.
  4. Sold goods for 90,000 cash.
    Dr Cash ₹90,000; Cr Sales ₹90,000. Cash comes in, so debit it. Sales is income, and income increases with a credit.
  5. Paid shop rent of 20,000 in cash.
    Dr Rent ₹20,000; Cr Cash ₹20,000. Rent is an expense, and expenses increase with a debit. Cash goes out, so credit it.
  6. Paid Sharma Traders 1,00,000 in cash.
    Dr Sharma Traders ₹1,00,000; Cr Cash ₹1,00,000. The amount owed to Sharma Traders falls, and liabilities decrease with a debit. Cash goes out, so credit it.

Check what you just learned

1. The journal is called the book of
  • Final entry
  • Summary
  • Original entry (correct)
  • Reference

Transactions are first entered in the journal.

2. Goods bought for 10,000: 4,000 cash and 6,000 on credit from Ravi. The credit side of the compound entry shows
  • Cash 4,000 and Ravi 6,000 (correct)
  • Cash 10,000
  • Ravi 10,000
  • Purchases 10,000

Purchases are debited 10,000; Cash and Ravi are credited by their respective parts.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping the narration. A journal entry without a reason cannot be audited.
  • Posting to the wrong side because the 'To' and 'By' words were confused.
Exam tip

Always journalise first, even if the question says 'prepare ledger accounts'. Examiners give marks for the journal as the working.

Try it yourself: What is meant by 'posting' and 'balancing' of ledger accounts?

Model answer. Posting is transferring each journal entry to the debit and credit accounts named in it. Balancing is totalling both sides of an account, finding the difference and carrying it down as the opening balance for the next period. The balance shows whether the account is a debit or credit position.

topics.title: Subsidiary books and the cash book
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain why a business keeps subsidiary books
  • Prepare a three-column cash book with contra entries and discounts
  • Describe the imprest system of petty cash

About 55 minutes

Journalising every sale and purchase one line at a time is slow. Businesses therefore divide the journal into subsidiary books by type of transaction: purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchase returns book, sales returns book, bills receivable and bills payable books, the cash book, and the journal proper for everything else. Each book is totalled periodically and the totals are posted to the ledger.

Subsidiary books at a glance
BookRecordsLedger posting
Purchases bookCredit purchases of goods for resaleEach supplier credited, Purchases debited with the total
Sales bookCredit sales of goodsEach customer debited, Sales credited with the total
Purchase returns bookGoods returned to suppliersSupplier debited, Purchase returns credited
Sales returns bookGoods returned by customersCustomer credited, Sales returns debited
Cash bookAll cash and bank receipts and paymentsItself a ledger account for cash and bank
Journal properOpening entries, adjustments, rectificationsAs per entry

The cash book is both a book of original entry and a ledger account. A three-column cash book has debit and credit sides, each with columns for discount, cash and bank. Discount allowed (to debtors who pay early) sits on the debit side; discount received (from creditors we pay early) sits on the credit side. A contra entry is a transaction that touches both cash and bank, such as depositing cash in the bank; it is recorded once on each side of the cash book and needs no ledger posting.

Petty cash handles small day-to-day expenses. Under the imprest system the petty cashier is given a fixed sum (the imprest) for a period. At the end of the period the amount spent is reimbursed so the imprest is restored. Expenses are recorded in an analytical petty cash book with a column for each type of expense.

In India

Many small Indian traders still record in a day book and bahi-khata. The same principles apply: record at the time of the transaction, keep a vouchers file, and balance the cash book every day.

Worked example

Three-column cash book, June 2026

Opening balances on 1 June: cash 25,000 and bank 1,00,000 (both debit). 3 Jun: received cheque from Rahul 19,500 in full settlement of 20,000 and deposited it. 6 Jun: paid Suresh by cheque 29,400 in full settlement of 30,000. 10 Jun: cash sales 15,000. 12 Jun: deposited cash in bank 10,000. 15 Jun: withdrew from bank for office use 5,000. 20 Jun: paid salaries in cash 12,000. Prepare the cash book and balance it.

  1. Debit side: Balance b/d (cash 25,000, bank 1,00,000); Rahul (discount allowed 500, bank 19,500); Sales (cash 15,000); Cash (contra, bank 10,000); Bank (contra, cash 5,000).
  2. Credit side: Suresh (discount received 600, bank 29,400); Bank (contra, cash 10,000); Salaries (cash 12,000); Cash (contra, bank 5,000).
  3. Cash column: debit 25,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = 45,000; credit 10,000 + 12,000 = 22,000; balance c/d = 23,000.
  4. Bank column: debit 1,00,000 + 19,500 + 10,000 = 1,29,500; credit 29,400 + 5,000 = 34,400; balance c/d = 95,100.
  5. Discount columns are not balanced. They are totalled and posted: discount allowed 500 to the debit of Discount Allowed A/c; discount received 600 to the credit of Discount Received A/c.

Answer. Cash in hand 23,000 and bank balance 95,100 at the end of the month.

Check what you just learned

1. Depositing cash into the bank is a
  • Contra entry (correct)
  • Compound entry
  • Rectification entry
  • Adjusting entry

Both cash and bank are in the cash book, so it is recorded on both sides of the cash book.

2. Discount allowed is recorded on the
  • Credit side of the cash book
  • Purchases book
  • Debit side of the cash book (correct)
  • Neither

Discount allowed to customers is an expense, shown on the debit side.

Common mistakes

  • Putting a contra entry on only one side of the cash book.
  • Balancing the discount columns. They are totalled only, because they are not cash or bank balances.
Exam tip

After you finish, check the cash and bank columns separately. Each should balance to a total that matches on both sides.

Try it yourself: Explain the imprest system of petty cash with an example.

Model answer. The petty cashier receives a fixed advance, say 5,000, for the month. Small expenses are paid from it and recorded in the petty cash book. At month end the head cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent. If 4,200 was spent, 4,200 is reimbursed and the imprest is back to 5,000. It limits misuse and gives control over small expenses.

topics.title: The trial balance
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Prepare a trial balance from ledger balances
  • State what a trial balance proves and what it does not prove

About 40 minutes

A trial balance is a list of all ledger account balances on a given date, arranged as debits and credits. Because every transaction has equal debits and credits, the two columns should agree. If they do, the books are arithmetically accurate. If they do not, an error exists and must be found before final accounts are prepared.

Where each balance goes

  • Debit column: assets, expenses and losses, drawings, closing stock if given as an adjustment later
  • Credit column: capital, liabilities, incomes and gains, provisions

The trial balance does not prove that the books are right. It will still balance if a transaction is left out completely, if the wrong account is used, if the same wrong amount is entered on both sides, or if one error is offset by another of equal size and opposite direction. So a balanced trial balance is necessary, not sufficient.

Tip

If the trial balance does not agree, first check the difference. If it divides evenly by 9 the cause is often a transposition (for example 54 written as 45). If it equals a single ledger balance, that balance may have been left out.

Worked example

Trial balance of Rohan Stationers at 30 April 2026

Ledger balances: Capital 3,00,000; Cash 2,55,000; Purchases 1,40,000; Sales 90,000; Gupta (debtor) 15,000; Verma & Co (creditor) 30,000; Rent 10,000. Prepare the trial balance.

  1. Debit balances: Cash 2,55,000; Purchases 1,40,000; Gupta 15,000; Rent 10,000. Total 4,20,000.
  2. Credit balances: Capital 3,00,000; Sales 90,000; Verma & Co 30,000. Total 4,20,000.
  3. Both columns agree, so the books are arithmetically accurate.
Trial balance (rupees)
AccountDebitCredit
Cash2,55,000
Purchases1,40,000
Gupta15,000
Rent10,000
Capital3,00,000
Sales90,000
Verma & Co30,000
Total4,20,0004,20,000

Answer. Trial balance totals: 4,20,000 on each side.

Key terms: ledger and trial balance

Journal
The book of original entry where transactions are first recorded in date order.
Ledger
The book of accounts in which journal entries are classified under account heads.
Double entry
Recording each transaction as equal debits and credits in two accounts.
Trial balance
A list of ledger balances used to check that total debits equal total credits.
Suspense account
A temporary account to hold the difference in the trial balance until errors are found.
Debtor
A person who owes money to the business.
Creditor
A person to whom the business owes money.

Check what you just learned

1. An error of complete omission
  • Is revealed by the trial balance
  • Is not revealed by the trial balance (correct)
  • Makes the debit total larger
  • Makes the credit total larger

Neither side is entered, so the totals still agree.

2. In a trial balance, drawings appear on the
  • Credit side
  • Either
  • It does not appear
  • Debit side (correct)

Drawings reduce capital and carry a debit balance.

Common mistakes

  • Putting a creditor's balance on the debit side because the word 'payment' appears in the question.
  • Forgetting to include opening balances.
Exam tip

Show a heading with the date, 'Trial balance as at 30 April 2026'. It is the standard presentation and costs nothing.

Try it yourself: List four errors that a trial balance cannot detect.

Model answer. Errors of complete omission, errors of commission such as posting to a wrong account of the same type, errors of principle such as treating capital expenditure as revenue, and compensating errors where one mistake cancels another.

topics.title: Errors and their rectification
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Classify accounting errors
  • Prepare rectifying journal entries
  • Use a suspense account to hold a trial balance difference

About 60 minutes

Types of accounting errors
TypeMeaningAffects the trial balance?
Error of omissionA transaction is left out wholly or partlyComplete omission: no. Partial (one side only): yes
Error of commissionWrong amount or wrong account of the same classWrong account: no. Wrong amount posted to one side: yes
Error of principleViolating an accounting principle, for example capital item treated as revenueNo
Compensating errorsTwo or more errors that cancel each otherNo

To correct an error, first decide what was done and what should have been done. Cancel the wrong effect and record the right one, using a single rectification entry. If the error affected one account only (a one-sided error), the other side of the entry is the suspense account. A suspense account is opened to hold the difference in the trial balance until its causes are found. Once all errors are rectified, the suspense balance should be nil.

Watch out

Never adjust the suspense account just to make the trial balance agree and forget it. The difference is a symptom. Each rectified error must be traced to a source and recorded in the books.

Worked example

Rectifying five errors with a suspense account

The trial balance of Mehra Traders was short on the debit side and the difference was put to a Suspense A/c. Later these errors were found: (1) Purchase of goods from Mehta for 5,000 was omitted from the books. (2) Rent of 3,000 paid was debited to the landlord's personal account. (3) Furniture purchased for 12,000 was debited to Purchases. (4) The sales book was overcast by 1,000. (5) Cash of 2,500 received from Ajay was credited to Ajay but not entered in the cash book. Pass rectifying entries and show the Suspense Account.

  1. (1) Complete omission, no suspense. Purchases Dr 5,000 / To Mehta 5,000.
  2. (2) Wrong account (commission). Rent Dr 3,000 / To Landlord 3,000.
  3. (3) Error of principle. Furniture Dr 12,000 / To Purchases 12,000.
  4. (4) Sales overcast by 1,000 means Sales was credited 1,000 too much. This extra credit is why the suspense account was debited. Sales Dr 1,000 / To Suspense 1,000.
  5. (5) Credit side only was done, so suspense was debited. Cash Dr 2,500 / To Suspense 2,500.
  6. Suspense account: debit side opening balance 3,500 (1,000 + 2,500). Credit side rectification 1,000 + 2,500 = 3,500. Balance nil.
Journal entries
EntryDebitAmountCreditAmount
1Purchases A/c Dr5,000To Mehta A/c5,000
2Rent A/c Dr3,000To Landlord A/c3,000
3Furniture A/c Dr12,000To Purchases A/c12,000
4Sales A/c Dr1,000To Suspense A/c1,000
5Cash A/c Dr2,500To Suspense A/c2,500

Answer. Suspense account closes to nil; the original trial balance difference was 3,500.

Check what you just learned

1. Purchase of a machine debited to Purchases A/c is an error of
  • Principle (correct)
  • Omission
  • Commission
  • Compensation

A capital item was treated as revenue: error of principle.

2. A suspense account is opened when
  • A new asset is bought
  • Goods are returned
  • Tax is paid
  • The trial balance does not agree (correct)

It temporarily holds the difference until errors are found.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the sides in a rectification entry. Always ask what should have been debited and credited.
  • Putting the whole suspense difference into one account at the start without tracing causes.
Exam tip

Set out each error in three short lines: what was done, what should have been done, the rectifying entry. It prevents sign mistakes.

Try it yourself: Give the rectifying entry when goods sold to Kiran for 4,000 were wrongly debited to Kamal.

Model answer. Kiran Dr 4,000 / To Kamal 4,000. This removes the debit from Kamal's account and places it in Kiran's account.

topics.title: Bank reconciliation statement
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain why the cash book and the pass book bank balances differ
  • Prepare a bank reconciliation statement (BRS)
  • Handle an overdraft balance

About 60 minutes

The bank's own record of your account is the pass book (or bank statement). Your record is the bank column of the cash book. They should agree but rarely do on any given date because each side learns of some transactions later. A BRS is a statement that explains the difference. It is prepared to catch errors, detect fraud and confirm the true bank balance.

Why the two balances differ
CauseIn the cash book?In the pass book?
Cheque issued but not yet presentedYesNo
Cheque deposited but not yet creditedYesNo
Bank charges, interest on loans, standing ordersNoYes
Direct deposits by customers (NEFT, UPI, RTGS)NoYes
Cheque dishonoured by the bankNo (until informed)Yes
Interest or dividend collected by the bankNoYes

A reliable method has two steps. First, correct the cash book for items the bank knows and you do not (charges, direct credits, dishonoured cheques) to reach an adjusted cash book balance. Second, reconcile the adjusted balance to the pass book balance by timing differences: add cheques issued but not presented, deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited. Remember that these directions flip when the bank column is an overdraft.

Tip

When the balance is an overdraft the signs reverse. Always check at the end: does the reconciled figure match the figure you were asked to reach?

Worked example

BRS starting from the cash book balance

On 31 March 2026 the bank column of the cash book showed a debit balance of 85,000. A comparison with the pass book showed: cheques issued 12,000 not yet presented; cheques deposited 8,000 not yet credited; bank charges 500 shown only in the pass book; a customer's direct deposit of 6,000 shown only in the pass book. Prepare the BRS and find the pass book balance.

  1. Cash book balance as given: 85,000 (Dr).
  2. Deduct bank charges (not yet in cash book): 85,000 - 500 = 84,500.
  3. Add direct deposit by customer: 84,500 + 6,000 = 90,500. This is the adjusted cash book balance.
  4. Add cheques issued but not yet presented (the bank has not yet paid them): 90,500 + 12,000 = 1,02,500.
  5. Deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited (the bank has not yet received them): 1,02,500 - 8,000 = 94,500.

Answer. The pass book shows a balance of 94,500 at the bank.

Check what you just learned

1. Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment are
  • Added to the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance (correct)
  • Deducted from the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance
  • Ignored
  • Entered in the journal

The bank has not yet paid them, so the pass book balance is higher than the cash book.

2. A bank charge shown only in the pass book requires
  • A cash book entry crediting the bank column (correct)
  • No action
  • A cash book entry debiting the bank column
  • A ledger entry only

The charge lowers your balance, so credit the bank column and debit Bank Charges.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the add and deduct directions for a credit balance when the cash book shows an overdraft.
  • Treating a BRS as a ledger account. It is a statement, not a double entry.
Exam tip

If the question gives the cash book balance, start from it and correct the cash book items first. If it gives the pass book balance, only timing items are needed.

Try it yourself: State four reasons for a difference between the cash book and the pass book balance.

Model answer. Cheques issued but not presented; cheques deposited but not credited; bank charges or interest recorded only by the bank; direct deposits or collections by the bank not yet entered in the cash book. Errors in either record also cause differences.

topics.title: Capital and revenue items
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Distinguish capital from revenue expenditure and receipts
  • Identify deferred revenue expenditure
  • Explain the effect of misclassification on profit and the balance sheet

About 40 minutes

Spending money does not automatically create an expense. If the benefit lasts beyond the current year, the spending is capital expenditure and is shown as an asset. If the benefit is used up within the year, it is revenue expenditure and is charged against income. The same distinction applies to receipts: sale of goods is a revenue receipt, while sale of a machine is a capital receipt.

Capital vs revenue
ItemTreatmentReason
Purchase of machinery for the factoryCapital expenditureBenefit lasts several years
Freight and installation to bring the machine into useCapital expenditureCost of getting the asset ready for use
Repairs to keep the machine runningRevenue expenditureMaintains existing capacity
Major overhaul that extends life or capacityCapital expenditureImproves the asset
Purchase of goods for resaleRevenue expenditureUsed up when goods are sold
Sale of old machineryCapital receiptDisposal of a fixed asset
Interest received on a bank depositRevenue receiptIncome from ordinary activity
Heavy advertising for a product launch spread over three yearsDeferred revenue expenditureBenefit extends over several periods; written off gradually

Misclassification distorts profit. Treating a capital item as revenue understates profit this year and overstates it in later years. Treating a revenue item as capital does the opposite and inflates profit and assets. Auditors watch this line closely.

Tip

Ask two questions. Does the benefit last more than one year? Does it add to or improve what the business can do? If yes to either, lean towards capital.

Check what you just learned

1. Wages paid for installing new machinery are
  • Revenue expenditure
  • Deferred revenue expenditure
  • Capital expenditure (correct)
  • Drawings

Installation wages form part of the machine's cost.

2. Proceeds from selling a delivery van are
  • Revenue receipt
  • Income
  • Capital receipt (correct)
  • Drawings

Sale of a fixed asset is a capital receipt.

Common mistakes

  • Treating all large amounts as capital. Size is not the test; benefit is.
  • Charging loose tools or small equipment as capital when the policy treats them as revenue because of materiality.
Exam tip

Write the reason in one clause beside each classification. Examiners award the reason, not just the label.

Try it yourself: A trader spent 50,000 on repairing a machine and 2,00,000 on increasing its capacity. How should each be treated?

Model answer. The 50,000 repair maintains the machine, so it is revenue expenditure and debited to the profit and loss account. The 2,00,000 increases capacity, so it is capital expenditure and added to the cost of the machine.

topics.title: Depreciation: straight-line and written-down-value
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain why depreciation is charged
  • Compute depreciation by the straight-line and written-down-value methods
  • Record depreciation, including part-year and disposal situations

About 60 minutes

Definition

Depreciation. The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life. It is a way of matching the cost of using an asset with the revenue it helps earn. It is not a fund of cash set aside for replacement.

Causes of depreciation

  • Wear and tear from use
  • Passage of time and expiry of legal rights, such as a lease or patent
  • Obsolescence, when new technology makes the asset out of date
  • Depletion of natural resources such as a mine
Formula · Straight-line method (SLM)

Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life in years

Equal charge every year. Often shown as a fixed percentage of cost.

Formula · Written-down-value method (WDV)

Annual depreciation = Rate % x Book value at start of the year

Charge is higher in early years and falls each year. Book value never reaches zero.

Both methods are allowed for companies. Schedule II to the Companies Act, 2013 gives indicative useful lives and requires a company to justify different lives it chooses. For income tax the Income-tax Act has its own block-wise WDV rates that may differ from the accounting rate; this is why a business may show two depreciation figures. Depreciation is calculated from the date the asset is available for use. If an asset is bought or sold during the year, charge depreciation for the part of the year it was used.

Accounting entries: (1) Depreciation A/c Dr, To Asset A/c, or (2) when a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account is kept, Depreciation A/c Dr, To Provision for Depreciation A/c. At the year end the depreciation account is closed to the profit and loss account. The asset appears in the balance sheet at cost less accumulated depreciation, which is its book value.

In India

Under the Companies Act, 2013 the amount of depreciation is based on useful life in Schedule II. Many small traders instead adopt the income-tax WDV rates in their books for simplicity; auditors accept this only when the rates do not distort the result materially.

Worked example

SLM and WDV on the same machine

A machine costing 5,00,000 was bought on 1 April 2023. Residual value 50,000, useful life 5 years. Calculate depreciation under (a) SLM and (b) WDV at 20% for the first three years, and show the book value at the end of each year.

  1. (a) SLM: (5,00,000 - 50,000) / 5 = 90,000 each year. Book value: end Y1 4,10,000; end Y2 3,20,000; end Y3 2,30,000.
  2. (b) WDV 20%: Year 1 = 20% of 5,00,000 = 1,00,000; book value 4,00,000. Year 2 = 20% of 4,00,000 = 80,000; book value 3,20,000. Year 3 = 20% of 3,20,000 = 64,000; book value 2,56,000.
  3. Comparison: after three years SLM has written off 2,70,000, WDV 2,44,000. WDV is heavier in Year 1 (1,00,000 vs 90,000) and lighter by Year 3 (64,000 vs 90,000).

Answer. SLM: 90,000 a year; WDV: 1,00,000, 80,000, 64,000.

Worked example

Part-year depreciation and sale at a loss

A firm closes its books on 31 March. It bought a computer on 1 October 2025 for 60,000 and charges SLM depreciation at 25% on cost. On 31 March 2027 it sold the computer for 20,000. Calculate depreciation for 2025-26 and 2026-27 and the profit or loss on sale.

  1. Year 2025-26: asset used 6 months. Depreciation = 60,000 x 25% x 6/12 = 7,500.
  2. Year 2026-27: full year = 60,000 x 25% = 15,000.
  3. Book value at sale = 60,000 - 7,500 - 15,000 = 37,500.
  4. Sale price 20,000, so loss on sale = 37,500 - 20,000 = 17,500.

Answer. Depreciation 7,500 and 15,000; loss on sale 17,500.

Straight-line against written-down value

Change the machine's cost, scrap value, life or the WDV rate and watch how the two methods write the asset down.

Adjust Cost of the machine, Scrap value, Useful life, WDV rate and see SLM charge every year, WDV charge in year 1, WDV charge in year 2 change.

Key terms: depreciation

Depreciation
Systematic allocation of the cost of an asset over its useful life.
Accumulated depreciation
Total depreciation charged on an asset since it was acquired.
Book value
Cost of an asset less accumulated depreciation.
Residual value
Estimated value of an asset at the end of its useful life.
Useful life
The period over which an asset is expected to be used.
Written-down value
Cost less accumulated depreciation; the book value on which WDV depreciation is charged.

Check what you just learned

1. Under WDV the depreciation charge each year
  • Falls (correct)
  • Stays constant
  • Rises
  • Is zero

The rate is applied to a falling book value.

2. Cost 3,00,000, scrap 30,000, life 9 years. SLM annual depreciation is
  • 33,333
  • 27,000
  • 30,000 (correct)
  • 36,000

(3,00,000 - 30,000) / 9 = 30,000.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the WDV rate to original cost every year; it is applied to the opening book value.
  • Forgetting to deduct residual value under SLM.
  • Charging a full year's depreciation on an asset bought a month before year end.
Exam tip

Present depreciation as a small table: year, opening value, depreciation, closing value. It makes checking easy and earns method marks even if one number slips.

Try it yourself: Why is depreciation called a non-cash expense? Does charging it create a fund for replacing the asset?

Model answer. No cash leaves the business when depreciation is charged; the cash was spent when the asset was bought. Charging depreciation reduces profit but does not by itself set aside any cash. A replacement fund exists only if the business separately invests an equal amount.
keyPoints: Depreciation: The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life.
Straight-line method (SLM): Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life in years
Written-down-value method (WDV): Annual depreciation = Rate % x Book value at start of the year
Exam tip: Present depreciation as a small table: year, opening value, depreciation, closing value.

topics.title: Inventory valuation: FIFO and weighted average
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain why closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value
  • Value closing stock and cost of goods sold by FIFO and weighted average
  • Explain the effect of the method on profit

About 55 minutes

Closing stock is the unsold goods at the end of the period. It is an asset in the balance sheet and it is subtracted from the cost of goods available so that only the cost of goods actually sold is matched with sales. Overstating closing stock raises this year's profit and lowers next year's by the same amount. That is why stock valuation is a classic route to profit manipulation.

Formula · Cost of goods sold

COGS = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock

Carriage inwards and other costs of bringing goods to the shop are added to purchases.

Accounting standards (AS 2 and Ind AS 2) require inventories to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). NRV is the estimated selling price less the cost of completion and the cost needed to make the sale. This is conservatism at work: if goods will sell for less than they cost, the loss is recognised at once. For cost, the standards permit the FIFO (first in, first out) or weighted average cost formulas. LIFO is not permitted under Ind AS 2 and is not used in India.

FIFO vs weighted average
FeatureFIFOWeighted average
AssumptionOldest goods are sold firstEvery unit has the average cost
Closing stockValued at latest purchase pricesValued at average cost
When prices are risingHigher closing stock, lower COGS, higher profitBetween FIFO and LIFO
When prices are fallingLower profit than weighted averageSmoother result
Worked example

FIFO and weighted average from the same data

A trader's records for January: Opening stock 100 units at 50. 10 Jan purchased 200 units at 55. 20 Jan purchased 100 units at 60. During the month 250 units were sold. Calculate closing stock and cost of goods sold by (a) FIFO and (b) weighted average (periodic).

  1. Goods available for sale: 100 + 200 + 100 = 400 units. Total cost = 100 x 50 + 200 x 55 + 100 x 60 = 5,000 + 11,000 + 6,000 = 22,000.
  2. Closing stock units = 400 - 250 = 150.
  3. (a) FIFO: the 150 closing units come from the latest purchases: 100 units at 60 + 50 units at 55 = 6,000 + 2,750 = 8,750. COGS = 22,000 - 8,750 = 13,250. Check: 100 x 50 + 150 x 55 = 5,000 + 8,250 = 13,250.
  4. (b) Weighted average cost per unit = 22,000 / 400 = 55. Closing stock = 150 x 55 = 8,250. COGS = 250 x 55 = 13,750.
  5. Difference: FIFO closing stock is 500 higher, so FIFO profit is 500 higher in a period of rising prices.

Answer. FIFO: closing stock 8,750, COGS 13,250. Weighted average: closing stock 8,250, COGS 13,750.

Worked example

Lower of cost and net realisable value

At year end, 100 units of a product cost 400 each. They can be sold for 450 each but 60 per unit must be spent on packing and delivery. At what value should they appear in the balance sheet?

  1. NRV per unit = 450 - 60 = 390.
  2. Cost per unit = 400. NRV is lower, so value at NRV.
  3. Closing stock value = 100 x 390 = 39,000 (against cost of 40,000). A loss of 1,000 is recognised now.

Answer. Closing stock is shown at 39,000.

Check what you just learned

1. Under Ind AS 2 inventory is valued at
  • Cost
  • Selling price
  • Lower of cost and net realisable value (correct)
  • Replacement cost

Inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV.

2. In a period of rising prices, FIFO gives
  • Lower profit than weighted average
  • Higher profit than weighted average (correct)
  • The same profit
  • No profit

Older, cheaper units go to COGS; recent, dearer units stay in closing stock.

Common mistakes

  • Valuing stock at selling price. It must be at cost or NRV.
  • In FIFO, taking the closing stock from the oldest purchase instead of the newest.
Exam tip

Write 'Goods available' first (units and cost), then the closing units, then value the closing stock. COGS is the balancing figure and doubles as a check.

Try it yourself: Why does an overstated closing stock affect the next year's profit?

Model answer. The closing stock of this year becomes the opening stock of next year. If it is overstated, this year's COGS is too low and profit too high; next year's opening stock is too high, so next year's COGS is too high and profit too low. The error reverses over two years.
keyPoints: Cost of goods sold: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock
Exam tip: Write 'Goods available' first (units and cost), then the closing units, then value the closing stock.

topics.title: Adjusting entries: outstanding, prepaid, accrued, advance, bad debts and provisions
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Apply the accrual concept to common year-end adjustments
  • Pass adjusting entries and show their effect on the accounts and the balance sheet
  • Compute bad debts and provision for doubtful debts

About 65 minutes

Cash moves on a different schedule from the events that cause it. Rent may be paid for 12 months in advance. Wages may be owed for the last week of March. Adjusting entries bring the books in line with the accrual concept so that each year bears the expenses that belong to it and earns the income that belongs to it.

The four basic adjustments
ItemMeaningEffect on P&LWhere it shows in the balance sheet
Outstanding expenseIncurred but not paidAdd to the expenseCurrent liability
Prepaid expensePaid but relates to the next yearDeduct from the expenseCurrent asset
Accrued incomeEarned but not receivedAdd to the incomeCurrent asset
Income received in advanceReceived for the next periodDeduct from the incomeCurrent liability

Bad debts are amounts owed by customers that will never be collected; they are written off as an expense. A provision for doubtful debts is an estimate of future bad debts from the debtors still on the books. It is charged to the profit and loss account this year even though the loss has not yet happened, in line with prudence. The usual order is: first write off the further bad debts, then calculate the provision on the remaining debtors, then charge only the increase over the old provision (or credit the profit and loss account with the decrease).

Formula · Charge for provision

New provision required - Old provision already in the books

A positive result is an additional charge; a negative result is a reduction credited to profit.

Watch out

Do not charge the full new provision every year. Only the change in the provision runs through the profit and loss account. The rest is already there from earlier years.

Worked example

Prepaid and outstanding expenses

On 1 October 2025 a firm paid rent of 60,000 for twelve months. Salaries paid during the year ended 31 March 2026 were 1,20,000, and a further 15,000 for March is still unpaid. Show the rent and salary charge to the profit and loss account and the balance sheet items.

  1. Rent: 12 months paid, 6 months (October to March) belong to this year. Expense = 60,000 x 6/12 = 30,000. Prepaid rent = 60,000 - 30,000 = 30,000 (current asset).
  2. Salaries: expense = 1,20,000 paid + 15,000 outstanding = 1,35,000. Outstanding salaries 15,000 appear as a current liability.

Answer. Rent 30,000 to P&L, prepaid 30,000; salaries 1,35,000 to P&L, outstanding 15,000.

Worked example

Bad debts and provision for doubtful debts

At 31 March 2026 sundry debtors were 1,00,000 before any adjustment. Bad debts of 4,000 are to be written off and a provision of 5% is to be kept on the remaining debtors. The provision for doubtful debts account already shows a credit balance of 3,000. Calculate the total charge to profit and loss.

  1. Debtors after writing off bad debts = 1,00,000 - 4,000 = 96,000.
  2. New provision required = 5% x 96,000 = 4,800.
  3. Old provision = 3,000, so additional provision = 4,800 - 3,000 = 1,800.
  4. Total charge to profit and loss = bad debts 4,000 + additional provision 1,800 = 5,800.
  5. Balance sheet: debtors 96,000 less provision 4,800 = 91,200.

Answer. Charge to P&L 5,800; debtors shown at 91,200 net.

Check what you just learned

1. Prepaid insurance is shown in the balance sheet as
  • A current liability
  • Capital
  • Drawings
  • A current asset (correct)

The firm has paid for a benefit still to come.

2. Old provision 6,000, new provision required 4,500. The profit and loss account is
  • Debited 1,500
  • Debited 4,500
  • Credited 6,000
  • Credited 1,500 (correct)

The provision is reduced by 1,500, which is a credit to profit.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a prepaid expense instead of deducting it.
  • Calculating the provision on gross debtors instead of debtors after writing off bad debts.
  • Forgetting that every adjustment has a balance sheet effect too.
Exam tip

Every adjustment appears twice in the final accounts: once in the profit and loss account (or trading account) and once in the balance sheet. If you only entered it once, the balance sheet will not agree.

Try it yourself: Rent paid during the year was 48,000, which includes 12,000 paid in advance for next year. What is the rent expense and where does the 12,000 appear?

Model answer. Rent expense for the year is 48,000 - 12,000 = 36,000. The 12,000 is prepaid rent, a current asset in the balance sheet.
keyPoints: Charge for provision: New provision required - Old provision already in the books
Exam tip: Every adjustment appears twice in the final accounts: once in the profit and loss account (or trading account) and once in the balance sheet.

topics.title: Trading account and profit and loss account
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain the purpose of final accounts
  • Prepare a trading account and a profit and loss account
  • Calculate gross profit and net profit

About 55 minutes

Final accounts are the statements prepared after the trial balance and adjustments to show the result of operations for the year and the position at the year end. They have three parts: the trading account, the profit and loss account, and the balance sheet. Together they answer the two questions every owner asks: did we make a profit, and what do we own and owe?

The trading account shows the direct result of buying and selling goods. On the debit side go opening stock, purchases (less returns), wages and carriage inwards, and other direct expenses. On the credit side go net sales (sales less returns) and closing stock. The balancing figure is gross profit when credits exceed debits, or gross loss when debits exceed credits.

Formula · Gross profit

Gross profit = Net sales + Closing stock - (Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses)

Equivalent to Net sales - Cost of goods sold.

The profit and loss account begins with gross profit on the credit side. It adds other incomes (commission, interest received) and deducts indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, bad debts). The balancing figure is net profit or net loss, which is transferred to the capital account. A sole proprietor does not pay himself a salary as an expense; his withdrawals are drawings, charged against capital.

What goes where
AccountDebit sideCredit side
Trading accountOpening stock, purchases less returns, wages, carriage inwards, other direct expensesNet sales, closing stock
Profit and loss accountSelling, administrative and financial expenses, depreciation, bad debts, provisionsGross profit, commission and interest received, other incomes
Watch out

Closing stock shown as an adjustment goes in the trading account (credit) and in the balance sheet (asset). If it is already in the trial balance, it appears only in the balance sheet.

Check what you just learned

1. Carriage inwards is debited to the
  • Profit and loss account
  • Balance sheet
  • Trading account (correct)
  • Capital account

It is a direct cost of getting goods to the shop.

2. A sole proprietor's own salary is
  • An expense in the profit and loss account
  • Drawings (correct)
  • An asset
  • A liability

The business and the owner are one for tax; withdrawals reduce capital.

Common mistakes

  • Putting carriage outwards in the trading account. It is a selling expense and belongs in profit and loss.
  • Treating drawings as an expense.
Exam tip

Present the trading account and profit and loss account in vertical form too. Indian universities accept both; check which your paper prefers.

Try it yourself: Why are sales returns deducted from sales in the trading account?

Model answer. Revenue is earned only on goods that customers keep. Returns reverse part of the sale, so net sales (sales minus returns) is the correct measure of revenue to match against cost of goods sold.
keyPoints: Gross profit: Gross profit = Net sales + Closing stock - (Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses)
Exam tip: Present the trading account and profit and loss account in vertical form too.

topics.title: The balance sheet
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain the purpose of the balance sheet
  • Classify assets and liabilities as current or non-current
  • Arrange a balance sheet in order of permanence and of liquidity

About 45 minutes

A balance sheet is a statement of assets, liabilities and capital at a particular date. It does not measure performance over a period; it is a photograph taken on one day. The accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) is the reason it must balance.

Classification
GroupMeaningExamples
Non-current (fixed) assetsHeld for long-term use, not for resaleLand, buildings, machinery, furniture, patents
Current assetsExpected to be converted to cash within a year or the operating cycleStock, debtors, cash, bank, prepaid expenses
Non-current liabilitiesRepayable after a yearLong-term loans, debentures
Current liabilitiesRepayable within a yearCreditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft
CapitalOwner's investment plus profits retained, less drawingsCapital account

Two arrangements are common. The order of permanence lists the least liquid assets first (land, machinery, then stock, debtors, cash) and the most permanent liabilities first (capital, then loans, then creditors). The order of liquidity does the opposite, starting with cash. Companies use a prescribed format in Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, which uses the current and non-current split.

Formula · Closing capital of a sole proprietor

Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit - Drawings (+ any additional capital introduced)

This is the figure that goes on the liability side of the balance sheet.

Tip

Show fixed assets at cost less accumulated depreciation, and debtors at gross value less the provision for doubtful debts. The net figures are what the balance sheet reports.

Key terms: the balance sheet

Balance sheet
A statement of assets, liabilities and capital on a given date.
Current asset
An asset expected to be converted into cash within a year or the operating cycle.
Prepaid expense
An expense paid in advance that relates to a future period.
Provision
An amount set aside for an expected liability or loss whose exact amount is uncertain.
Drawings
Cash or goods taken out of the business by the owner for personal use.
Final accounts
Trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet.
Gross profit
Net sales less cost of goods sold.

Check what you just learned

1. Under the order of liquidity, the first asset listed is
  • Land
  • Machinery
  • Cash (correct)
  • Goodwill

Cash is the most liquid asset and comes first.

2. Bank overdraft is classified as
  • Non-current asset
  • Capital
  • Non-current liability
  • Current liability (correct)

An overdraft is repayable on demand.

Common mistakes

  • Setting outstanding expenses against the expense on the asset side. It is a liability.
  • Deducting drawings from profit in the profit and loss account instead of from capital.
Exam tip

Always cross-check: the balance sheet total of assets must equal the total of capital plus liabilities. If it does not, the error is in one of the adjustments or in the profit figure.

Try it yourself: Differentiate between a trial balance and a balance sheet.

Model answer. A trial balance lists all ledger balances on a date to test arithmetical accuracy; it includes expenses and incomes. A balance sheet lists only assets, liabilities and capital at a date and shows the financial position after adjustments and after transferring profit to capital.
keyPoints: Closing capital of a sole proprietor: Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit - Drawings (+ any additional capital introduced)
Exam tip: Always cross-check: the balance sheet total of assets must equal the total of capital plus liabilities.

topics.title: Final accounts with adjustments: a complete example
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Prepare a trading account, a profit and loss account and a balance sheet from a trial balance with adjustments
  • Check that the balance sheet balances

About 80 minutes

This lesson works through a full question, the way a university paper sets it. Work through it with a pencil. The order that never fails is: (1) trading account, (2) profit and loss account, (3) balance sheet. For each adjustment ask where it appears: it normally affects one statement of results and the balance sheet.

A checklist for every final accounts question

  1. Read all adjustments first and mark which account each one affects
  2. Net the sales and purchases for returns before the trading account
  3. Add outstanding and subtract prepaid expenses in the profit and loss account
  4. Compute depreciation and the net provision for doubtful debts
  5. Transfer net profit to capital and subtract drawings
  6. Match the total of the two sides of the balance sheet
Worked example

Meera Garments, year ended 31 March 2026

Trial balance debits: Opening stock 80,000; Purchases 6,40,000; Sales returns 20,000; Wages 60,000; Carriage inwards 10,000; Salaries 1,20,000; Rent 48,000; Office expenses 36,000; Insurance 12,000; Debtors 1,50,000; Cash in hand 15,000; Cash at bank 1,25,000; Furniture 1,00,000; Machinery 2,00,000; Drawings 60,000; Bad debts 6,000; Advertising 24,000. Credits: Sales 11,60,000; Purchase returns 30,000; Creditors 1,10,000; Provision for doubtful debts 4,000; Commission received 12,000; Capital 3,90,000. Adjustments: (a) closing stock 95,000; (b) outstanding salaries 10,000; (c) prepaid insurance 3,000; (d) depreciate furniture 10% and machinery 15% (on the balances given); (e) write off further bad debts of 5,000 and keep the provision at 5% on the remaining debtors; (f) commission received in advance 2,000. Prepare the trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet.

  1. Trading account debits: opening stock 80,000 + net purchases (6,40,000 - 30,000 = 6,10,000) + wages 60,000 + carriage inwards 10,000 = 7,60,000.
  2. Trading account credits: net sales (11,60,000 - 20,000 = 11,40,000) + closing stock 95,000 = 12,35,000. Gross profit = 12,35,000 - 7,60,000 = 4,75,000.
  3. Profit and loss debits: salaries 1,20,000 + outstanding 10,000 = 1,30,000; rent 48,000; office expenses 36,000; insurance 12,000 - 3,000 = 9,000; advertising 24,000; bad debts 6,000 + 5,000 = 11,000; additional provision (5% x (1,50,000 - 5,000) = 7,250, less existing 4,000) = 3,250; depreciation 10,000 + 30,000 = 40,000. Total = 3,01,250.
  4. Profit and loss credits: gross profit 4,75,000 + commission (12,000 - 2,000 = 10,000) = 4,85,000. Net profit = 4,85,000 - 3,01,250 = 1,83,750.
  5. Closing capital = 3,90,000 + 1,83,750 - 60,000 = 5,13,750.
  6. Balance sheet liabilities: capital 5,13,750 + creditors 1,10,000 + outstanding salaries 10,000 + commission received in advance 2,000 = 6,35,750.
  7. Balance sheet assets: closing stock 95,000 + debtors (1,45,000 - 7,250 = 1,37,750) + prepaid insurance 3,000 + cash 15,000 + bank 1,25,000 + furniture (1,00,000 - 10,000 = 90,000) + machinery (2,00,000 - 30,000 = 1,70,000) = 6,35,750.

Check what you just learned

1. Net profit is transferred to
  • Trading account
  • Drawings account
  • Debtors
  • Capital account (correct)

For a sole proprietor, net profit increases capital.

2. If closing stock appears as an adjustment, it is entered
  • Only in the balance sheet
  • Only in the trading account
  • In the profit and loss account
  • In the trading account and in the balance sheet (correct)

It appears on the credit side of trading and as a current asset.

Common mistakes

  • Applying depreciation to the net book value when the question says 'on the balances given'. Use the figures stated.
  • Putting the additional provision rather than the new provision in the profit and loss account.
Exam tip

Write the adjusted figure and its calculation beside each item (for example 'Insurance 12,000 - 3,000 = 9,000'). Marks are awarded for working.

Try it yourself: Why does a balance sheet balance only after net profit is transferred to capital?

Model answer. Before the transfer, the trial balance carries incomes and expenses as separate nominal accounts. Closing them into the profit and loss account and transferring the net profit to capital brings the effect of all revenue transactions into the owner's capital, which restores the equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

topics.title: Accounts of non-profit organisations
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain how non-profit accounting differs from that of a trader
  • Prepare an income and expenditure account from a receipts and payments account
  • Prepare the balance sheet of a non-profit organisation

About 70 minutes

Clubs, societies, trusts and many NGOs exist to serve their members or a cause, not to make profit for owners. They do not usually keep full double-entry books for trading. At the year end they prepare three statements: a receipts and payments account, an income and expenditure account and a balance sheet. Donors, regulators and members read these same statements.

The three statements
StatementWhat it isBasis
Receipts and payments accountA summary of the cash book for the year, opening balance to closing balanceCash basis. Includes capital and revenue items, no adjustments
Income and expenditure accountThe equivalent of the profit and loss account; shows surplus or deficitAccrual basis. Only revenue items of the year, with adjustments
Balance sheetAssets and liabilities at the year endAccrual basis. The surplus is added to the general (capital) fund

Three points explain most of the work. First, capital receipts (such as a donation for a building fund, or an entrance fee the society treats as capital) and capital payments (such as buying equipment) do not go in the income and expenditure account; they go in the balance sheet. Second, subscriptions are an income of the year to which they relate, so they are adjusted for amounts outstanding and in advance. Third, the opposite of profit is called a surplus or deficit, and it is added to or deducted from the general fund (capital fund).

Formula · Income from subscriptions for the year

Subscriptions received - Opening outstanding + Closing outstanding - Advance received for next year (+ opening advance if any)

Adjust for amounts relating to other years so that the income matches the year.

In India

Registered Indian trusts and societies prepare statements in this format, and charitable trusts under the Income-tax Act are also expected to account for corpus funds separately. Donors often ask for the statement of income and expenditure along with the utilisation certificate for specific grants.

Worked example

Green Park Sports Club, year ended 31 March 2026

Receipts and payments account: Receipts - opening cash 40,000; subscriptions 2,10,000; donation for building fund 1,00,000; interest on investments 18,000. Payments - salaries 1,20,000; sports equipment purchased 60,000; electricity 24,000; printing and stationery 16,000. Additional information: subscriptions outstanding at the start 10,000 (received this year and included above); outstanding at the end 15,000; subscriptions received in advance at the end 6,000; salaries outstanding at the end 10,000. Sports equipment at the start was 2,00,000 and is to be depreciated at 10% on the total including additions. The investments of 1,80,000 are unchanged. Prepare the income and expenditure account and the balance sheet.

  1. Closing cash = total receipts (40,000 + 2,10,000 + 1,00,000 + 18,000 = 3,68,000) minus total payments (1,20,000 + 60,000 + 24,000 + 16,000 = 2,20,000) = 1,48,000.
  2. Subscription income = 2,10,000 - 10,000 (belongs to last year) + 15,000 (outstanding this year) - 6,000 (advance for next year) = 2,09,000.
  3. Salaries expense = 1,20,000 + 10,000 outstanding = 1,30,000.
  4. Depreciation on equipment = 10% x (2,00,000 + 60,000) = 26,000.
  5. Income and expenditure: income = subscriptions 2,09,000 + interest 18,000 = 2,27,000. Expenditure = salaries 1,30,000 + electricity 24,000 + printing 16,000 + depreciation 26,000 = 1,96,000. Surplus = 31,000.
  6. The building fund donation of 1,00,000 and the purchase of equipment are capital items. They do not enter the income and expenditure account.
  7. Opening general fund = assets (cash 40,000 + subscriptions outstanding 10,000 + equipment 2,00,000 + investments 1,80,000 = 4,30,000) with no outside liabilities.
  8. Closing balance sheet - liabilities: general fund (4,30,000 + 31,000 = 4,61,000), building fund 1,00,000, subscriptions in advance 6,000, outstanding salaries 10,000 = 5,77,000. Assets: cash 1,48,000, subscriptions outstanding 15,000, equipment (2,60,000 - 26,000 = 2,34,000), investments 1,80,000 = 5,77,000.

Answer. Surplus 31,000; general fund 4,61,000; balance sheet total 5,77,000.

Check what you just learned

1. Which of the following is NOT recorded in the income and expenditure account?
  • Subscriptions for the year
  • Salaries for the year
  • Purchase of a sports van (correct)
  • Interest on investments

Purchase of a van is a capital payment.

2. The surplus of a non-profit organisation is added to the
  • Cash
  • Capital fund (general fund) (correct)
  • Bank overdraft
  • Drawings

A surplus increases the general fund.

Common mistakes

  • Including donations for a specific fund or capital items in the income and expenditure account.
  • Forgetting to adjust subscriptions for opening and closing outstanding or advance.
  • Using the same figure for subscriptions in both statements without adjustment.
Exam tip

When a question gives only a receipts and payments account, compute subscription income with a one-line working before anything else. It prevents the most common error.

Try it yourself: Distinguish the receipts and payments account from the income and expenditure account.

Model answer. The receipts and payments account is a summary of cash transactions that includes capital and revenue items and is not adjusted for outstanding or advance amounts. The income and expenditure account includes only revenue items of the year, on an accrual basis, and shows the surplus or deficit.
keyPoints: Income from subscriptions for the year: Subscriptions received - Opening outstanding + Closing outstanding - Advance received for next year (+ opening advance if any)
