topics.title: Bills of exchange
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Define a bill of exchange and identify its parties
  • Pass entries for acceptance, discounting, endorsement, maturity and dishonour
  • Calculate the due date and the discount

About 60 minutes

Definition

Bill of exchange. A written, signed, unconditional order by one person (the drawer) directing another (the drawee) to pay a certain sum to a named person (the payee) on demand or at a fixed future time. When the drawee signs it as accepted, it becomes a binding instrument. It is governed by the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

The usual case is a seller (drawer) who has sold goods on credit and draws a bill on the buyer (drawee). The buyer accepts it. The bill is then held by the seller until the due date, endorsed to a creditor, or discounted with a bank. Due date is the end of the term plus three days of grace; if that day is a public holiday the bill is due on the preceding business day.

Journal entries in the drawer's books
EventEntry
Credit saleDrawee Dr / To Sales
Bill acceptedBills Receivable Dr / To Drawee
Bill retained and paid at maturityBank Dr / To Bills Receivable
Bill discounted with bankBank Dr (net proceeds), Discount Dr / To Bills Receivable
Bill endorsed to a creditorCreditor Dr / To Bills Receivable
Bill dishonouredDrawee Dr (bill amount plus noting charges) / To Bank, or To Bills Receivable
Journal entries in the drawee's books
EventEntry
Credit purchasePurchases Dr / To Drawer
Bill acceptedDrawer Dr / To Bills Payable
Payment on due dateBills Payable Dr / To Bank
Bill dishonouredBills Payable Dr / To Drawer (plus noting charges if borne)
Formula · Discount on a bill

Discount = Bill amount x Rate of discount x Period / 12

Period is the number of months from the date of discounting to the due date.

Watch out

A bill that has been discounted leaves a contingent liability: if the drawee fails to pay, the bank recovers from the drawer. Disclose it in the notes; it is not a liability in the balance sheet unless dishonoured.

Worked example

Discounting and dishonour of a bill

Ravi sold goods worth 50,000 to Sunil. Ravi drew a three-month bill on Sunil, who accepted it. Ravi immediately discounted the bill with his bank at 12% per annum. On the due date Sunil failed to pay, and the bank debited Ravi with the bill amount and noting charges of 200. Pass the journal entries in Ravi's books.

  1. Sale: Sunil Dr 50,000 / To Sales 50,000.
  2. Acceptance: Bills Receivable Dr 50,000 / To Sunil 50,000.
  3. Discount = 50,000 x 12% x 3/12 = 1,500; net proceeds = 48,500. Entry: Bank Dr 48,500, Discount Dr 1,500 / To Bills Receivable 50,000.
  4. Dishonour: the bank recovers 50,200 from Ravi. Sunil Dr 50,200 / To Bank 50,200. Sunil's account is again debited with the bill amount and the charges.
Journal entries
EntryDebitAmountCreditAmount
saleSunil A/c Dr50,000To Sales A/c50,000
acceptanceBills Receivable A/c Dr50,000To Sunil A/c50,000
discountBank A/c Dr48,500To Bills Receivable A/c50,000
Discount A/c Dr1,500
dishonourSunil A/c Dr50,200To Bank A/c50,200

Answer. Discount 1,500; net proceeds 48,500; Sunil owes 50,200 after dishonour.

Key terms: bills of exchange

Bill of exchange
A written, unconditional order from the drawer to the drawee to pay a certain sum on a fixed date to the payee.
Drawer
The person who writes a bill of exchange.
Drawee
The person who is ordered to pay a bill of exchange.
Discount allowed
A reduction given to customers who pay early; an expense.
Discount received
A reduction obtained from suppliers for early payment; an income.

Check what you just learned

1. The drawee of a bill is
  • The person who must pay (correct)
  • The person who orders payment
  • The person who receives payment
  • The bank

The drawee accepts the order and pays the bill.

2. Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, days of grace for a bill payable after a fixed period are
  • None
  • Seven
  • Three (correct)
  • Ten

Three days of grace are added to arrive at the due date.

Common mistakes

  • Calculating discount on the discount-adjusted amount instead of the face value.
  • Forgetting the days of grace.
Exam tip

Draw a small timeline: date of drawing, date of acceptance, date of discounting, due date. It prevents mistakes in the period for discount.

Try it yourself: Why is a discounted bill a contingent liability for the drawer?

Model answer. After discounting, the bank has paid the drawer, but if the drawee does not pay on the due date, the bank has a right of recourse against the drawer. Until the bill is honoured, the drawer may have to pay, so it is disclosed as a contingent liability.
keyPoints: Bill of exchange: A written, signed, unconditional order by one person (the drawer) directing another (the drawee) to pay a certain sum to a named person (the payee) on demand or at a fixed future time.
Discount on a bill: Discount = Bill amount x Rate of discount x Period / 12
Exam tip: Draw a small timeline: date of drawing, date of acceptance, date of discounting, due date.

topics.title: Consignment accounts
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Define consignment and distinguish it from a sale
  • Prepare the consignment account in the consignor's books
  • Value unsold stock and treat normal and abnormal losses

About 70 minutes

In a consignment the consignor sends goods to an agent, the consignee, to sell on the consignor's behalf. Ownership stays with the consignor until the goods are sold to the final buyer. The consignee earns a commission and is reimbursed for approved expenses. A consignment is not a sale, so no profit is recognised on goods sent; the consignor records the result only after the consignee reports sales.

The consignee sends an account sales: a statement of goods sold, expenses incurred, commission and the balance remitted. In the consignor's books a Consignment account is kept, showing the goods sent at cost, the consignor's own expenses, and the consignee's expenses and commission on the debit side; sales proceeds and the closing stock on the credit side. The balancing figure is the profit or loss on consignment.

Valuing unsold stock on consignment

  • Stock is valued at cost plus a proportionate share of the expenses incurred by the consignor to bring goods to the consignee (freight, insurance)
  • The consignee's selling expenses (godown rent, advertising) are not added, because they are not incurred to bring goods to the place of sale
  • A normal loss (evaporation, breakage that is unavoidable) is not shown separately; the cost per unit is raised by spreading cost over the remaining units
  • An abnormal loss (fire, theft, negligence) is valued at cost including proportionate expenses and charged to profit and loss, with a credit to the consignment account
Formula · Value of closing stock on consignment

Unsold units x cost per unit + Consignor's expenses x (Unsold units / Units sent)

Consignee's expenses are excluded.

Tip

To keep the consignment account honest, treat goods sent on consignment as goods taken out of your normal trading stock: Consignment Dr / To Goods Sent on Consignment. At the year end, Goods Sent on Consignment is transferred to the trading account.

Worked example

Profit on consignment

Anand & Co. consigned 1,000 units to Bhatia at cost 100 per unit. Anand paid freight 5,000 and insurance 2,000. Bhatia sold 800 units at 130 each for cash, paid godown rent 3,000 and is entitled to commission of 5% on sales. Prepare the consignment account, find the value of unsold stock and the amount Bhatia remits.

  1. Goods sent = 1,000 x 100 = 1,00,000. Consignor's expenses = 5,000 + 2,000 = 7,000.
  2. Sales = 800 x 130 = 1,04,000. Commission = 5% x 1,04,000 = 5,200.
  3. Unsold units = 200. Value = 200 x 100 + 7,000 x 200/1,000 = 20,000 + 1,400 = 21,400. The godown rent is excluded.
  4. Consignment account debits: goods sent 1,00,000 + consignor's expenses 7,000 + consignee's godown rent 3,000 + commission 5,200 = 1,15,200.
  5. Consignment account credits: sales 1,04,000 + closing stock 21,400 = 1,25,400.
  6. Profit on consignment = 1,25,400 - 1,15,200 = 10,200.
  7. Bhatia remits = sales 1,04,000 - godown rent 3,000 - commission 5,200 = 95,800.

Answer. Closing stock 21,400; profit 10,200; Bhatia remits 95,800.

Worked example

Normal and abnormal loss

Goods of 1,000 units were consigned at an invoice cost of 90,000. The consignor spent 8,000 on freight and insurance. A normal loss of 20 units was expected and 50 units were destroyed by fire in transit. Find the cost per unit and the value of the abnormal loss.

  1. Total cost = 90,000 + 8,000 = 98,000.
  2. Units expected to be available = 1,000 - 20 (normal loss) = 980.
  3. Cost per unit = 98,000 / 980 = 100.
  4. Abnormal loss = 50 units x 100 = 5,000. It is credited to the consignment account and charged to the profit and loss account (less insurance claim, if any).

Answer. Cost per unit 100; abnormal loss 5,000.

Key terms: consignment

Consignment
Sending goods to an agent for sale while the sender keeps ownership.
Account sales
A statement sent by a consignee to the consignor showing goods sold, expenses, commission and the balance due.
Closing stock
Unsold goods at the end of the period.
Net realisable value
Estimated selling price less the cost of completion and selling.

Check what you just learned

1. In a consignment, ownership of the goods rests with
  • The consignor (correct)
  • The consignee
  • The final buyer
  • The bank

The consignee is only an agent.

2. Unsold stock on consignment is valued at
  • Selling price
  • Cost plus consignee's selling expenses
  • NRV only
  • Cost plus proportionate consignor's expenses (correct)

Only expenses to bring the goods to the consignee's place are added.

Common mistakes

  • Including godown rent in the value of closing stock.
  • Treating goods sent on consignment as a sale to the consignee.
Exam tip

Compute stock last. First write the consignment debits and credits except the closing stock, and see what the profit would be before stock; then include stock.

Try it yourself: Differentiate between sale and consignment.

Model answer. In a sale, ownership passes to the buyer, who is liable to pay the price and bears the risk. In a consignment, ownership remains with the consignor and the consignee is only an agent who sells and earns a commission. A sale creates a debtor; a consignment does not.
keyPoints: Value of closing stock on consignment: Unsold units x cost per unit + Consignor's expenses x (Unsold units / Units sent)
Exam tip: Compute stock last.
Define consignment and distinguish it from a sale

topics.title: Joint venture accounts
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Define a joint venture and distinguish it from a partnership
  • Prepare a joint venture account when co-venturers keep separate sets of books
  • Settle the accounts between co-venturers

About 55 minutes

A joint venture is a temporary business between two or more persons for a single project or a short period, with profit and loss shared in an agreed ratio. It ends when the project ends and no firm name or continuing relationship follows. This is the key difference from a partnership, which is a continuing business.

Three ways of keeping the accounts exist. If one co-venturer keeps all books, a joint venture account is kept by him. If a separate bank account is opened, joint bank account entries are made. If each co-venturer records only his own transactions, each opens a joint venture account in his own books and a co-venturer's account for the other. The last method is the most common in exams, and the one illustrated here.

What the Joint Venture Account shows

  • Debit side: goods purchased, expenses incurred by the co-venturer, commission, and profit transferred to the co-venturer's capital
  • Credit side: sales, stock taken over by a co-venturer, unsold stock valued at cost
  • The balance is profit or loss, shared in the agreed ratio
Tip

In a joint venture each co-venturer only records his own part. At the end the venture is complete when the one holding the sale proceeds pays the other what is due. The total of what each party is due equals the total cash in the venture.

Worked example

Joint venture between A and B

A and B enter into a joint venture sharing profits in the ratio 3:2. A buys goods for 1,20,000 and spends 6,000 on expenses. B sells all the goods except those taken by A at 10,000, receives 1,90,000 and spends 4,000 on expenses. Find the profit, each party's share and the amount B must remit to A.

  1. Income: sales 1,90,000 + goods taken over by A 10,000 = 2,00,000.
  2. Costs: purchases 1,20,000 + A's expenses 6,000 + B's expenses 4,000 = 1,30,000.
  3. Profit = 2,00,000 - 1,30,000 = 70,000. A's share (3/5) = 42,000; B's share (2/5) = 28,000.
  4. B holds sale proceeds net of his expenses = 1,90,000 - 4,000 = 1,86,000. B keeps his profit share 28,000 and remits the rest.
  5. B remits to A = 1,86,000 - 28,000 = 1,58,000.
  6. Cross-check: A's total due = purchases 1,20,000 + expenses 6,000 + profit 42,000 - goods taken over 10,000 = 1,58,000. The two methods agree.

Answer. Profit 70,000 (A 42,000, B 28,000); B remits 1,58,000 to A.

Check what you just learned

1. A joint venture differs from partnership because it
  • Has no profit sharing
  • Cannot have two persons
  • Needs a firm name
  • Is formed for a specific purpose and ends when it is complete (correct)

A joint venture is temporary and project-specific.

2. Goods taken over by a co-venturer are credited to
  • Capital
  • Joint venture account (correct)
  • Cash
  • Sales

They are treated as income of the venture and debited to the co-venturer.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the sum received by one co-venturer as his own profit.
  • Forgetting to include goods taken over by a co-venturer as income.
Exam tip

Always do the check: total due to A = A's own cost + A's profit share - any goods A took. It must match the amount B remits.

Try it yourself: List the points of difference between consignment and joint venture.

Model answer. A consignment is an agency: one party owns the goods and the other sells for commission. A joint venture involves two or more persons sharing profit and loss, each contributing funds or services. Consignment continues as an arrangement; a joint venture is for a specific project. The consignee is paid commission; co-venturers share profit.

topics.title: Why and how financial statements are analysed
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain the purpose and limitations of financial statement analysis
  • Prepare comparative and common-size statements
  • Interpret trends

About 45 minutes

A single year's profit figure tells you little. Is 1,80,000 good? It depends on last year, on sales, on capital employed and on similar businesses. Analysis converts raw statement figures into comparisons that answer questions. Its tools are comparative statements (the same line over time), common-size statements (every line as a percentage of a base) and ratios (relationships between lines).

Main tools of analysis
ToolHow it worksTypical use
Comparative statement (horizontal)Show amounts for two or more years side by side with absolute and percentage changeSpot growth and deterioration over time
Common-size statement (vertical)Express each item as a percentage of sales (P&L) or total assets (balance sheet)Compare firms of different size, or one firm over time
Ratio analysisDivide one figure by another that is relatedJudge liquidity, solvency, profitability, efficiency
Trend analysisIndex a series to a base year (base = 100)See long-term movement
Cash flow analysisTrace the movement of cashTest whether profits are turning into cash

Limits matter. Statements show historical cost, not market value. Accounting policies differ between firms. Inflation distorts comparisons across years. A ratio is only meaningful against something: the same firm's past, the industry, or a stated target. The 2:1 current ratio often quoted in textbooks is a rule of thumb, and many healthy businesses (for example retailers with fast-moving stock) operate with lower figures.

Worked example

Comparative and common-size income statement

A firm reports: Sales 10,00,000 (2024-25) and 12,00,000 (2025-26); Cost of goods sold 6,00,000 and 7,50,000; Other expenses 2,50,000 and 2,70,000. Prepare a comparative statement with percentage change, and common-size figures for gross profit and net profit.

  1. Gross profit: 2024-25 = 10,00,000 - 6,00,000 = 4,00,000; 2025-26 = 12,00,000 - 7,50,000 = 4,50,000. Change = 50,000, or 12.5%.
  2. Net profit: 2024-25 = 4,00,000 - 2,50,000 = 1,50,000; 2025-26 = 4,50,000 - 2,70,000 = 1,80,000. Change = 30,000, or 20%.
  3. Sales grew 20%, cost of goods sold grew 25%, other expenses grew 8%.
  4. Common-size: gross profit margin 40% in 2024-25 and 37.5% in 2025-26. Net profit margin 15% and 15%.
  5. Reading: sales grew faster than gross profit, so the gross margin slipped by 2.5 points. The firm kept net margin steady by controlling other expenses.

Answer. Net profit up 20%; gross margin 40% to 37.5%; net margin steady at 15%.

Check what you just learned

1. A common-size statement expresses each item as a percentage of
  • Last year's value
  • Net profit
  • A common base such as sales or total assets (correct)
  • Capital

That is what makes firms and years comparable.

2. Comparing the same line across years is
  • Horizontal analysis (correct)
  • Vertical analysis
  • Ratio analysis
  • Cash flow analysis

Horizontal analysis tracks change over time.

Common mistakes

  • Calculating the percentage change on the new year instead of the base year.
  • Comparing firms of different industries as if they were similar.
Exam tip

Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100. State the base year in the question text. This one formula is tested more than any other in this unit.

Try it yourself: State three limitations of financial statement analysis.

Model answer. Statements show historical cost, so values may be outdated; different firms use different accounting policies, which reduces comparability; inflation distorts year-to-year comparisons; and ratios ignore qualitative factors such as management quality.
keyPoints: Exam tip: Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100.

topics.title: Ratio analysis
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Compute liquidity, solvency, profitability and activity ratios
  • Interpret each ratio in words a manager or banker would use

About 70 minutes

Core ratios
GroupRatioFormulaWhat it tells you
LiquidityCurrent ratioCurrent assets / Current liabilitiesCan short-term dues be paid from short-term assets?
LiquidityQuick ratio(Current assets - Stock - Prepaid) / Current liabilitiesCan dues be met without selling stock?
SolvencyDebt-equity ratioLong-term debt / Shareholders' funds (or total debt / equity)How heavily is the business financed by borrowing?
SolvencyInterest coverageEBIT / Interest expenseHow many times profit covers interest
ProfitabilityGross profit ratioGross profit / Net sales x 100Margin on goods before overheads
ProfitabilityNet profit ratioNet profit / Net sales x 100Margin after all expenses
ProfitabilityReturn on equityNet profit / Shareholders' funds x 100Return earned for owners
ProfitabilityReturn on capital employed (ROCE)EBIT / (Equity + Long-term debt) x 100Return on all long-term funds
ActivityStock turnoverCOGS / Average stockHow many times stock is sold and replaced
ActivityDebtors turnover and collection periodNet credit sales / Average debtors; 365 / turnoverHow quickly customers pay
ActivityCreditors payment period365 x Average creditors / Credit purchasesHow long the firm takes to pay suppliers

Ratios work in groups. A high current ratio may mean strong liquidity or may mean idle stock. A rising return on equity may mean better operations or more borrowing; check debt-equity before celebrating. A long debtor collection period with a short creditor payment period signals a squeeze on cash. Always read ratios against the firm's own history and its industry, and say what the number means for decisions.

Watch out

Use average balances (opening plus closing, divided by two) for turnover ratios when both are available. If only the closing balance is given, say so in your working.

Worked example

A full ratio set for Kiran Foods Ltd.

From the 2025-26 statements: Net sales (all on credit) 12,00,000; Cost of goods sold 8,40,000; Net profit after 20,000 interest 1,20,000 (ignore tax); Current assets 4,50,000 of which stock 1,50,000 (opening stock was also 1,50,000); Non-current assets 6,00,000; Current liabilities 2,50,000; Long-term loan 3,00,000; Shareholders' funds 5,00,000; Debtors 1,20,000. Compute the key ratios.

  1. Check: total assets = 4,50,000 + 6,00,000 = 10,50,000. Total funds = equity 5,00,000 + loan 3,00,000 + current liabilities 2,50,000 = 10,50,000. They balance.
  2. Current ratio = 4,50,000 / 2,50,000 = 1.8 : 1.
  3. Quick ratio = (4,50,000 - 1,50,000) / 2,50,000 = 1.2 : 1.
  4. Gross profit = 12,00,000 - 8,40,000 = 3,60,000; gross profit ratio = 30%.
  5. Net profit ratio = 1,20,000 / 12,00,000 = 10%.
  6. Stock turnover = 8,40,000 / 1,50,000 (average of opening and closing) = 5.6 times.
  7. Debtors turnover = 12,00,000 / 1,20,000 = 10 times; collection period = 365 / 10 = 36.5 days.
  8. Debt-equity ratio = 3,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 0.6 : 1.
  9. EBIT = 1,20,000 + 20,000 = 1,40,000; interest coverage = 1,40,000 / 20,000 = 7 times.
  10. Return on equity = 1,20,000 / 5,00,000 = 24%.
  11. ROCE = 1,40,000 / (5,00,000 + 3,00,000) = 17.5%.
  12. Reading: the firm pays its short-term dues comfortably (quick ratio 1.2), collects from customers in about five weeks, and covers interest seven times. Borrowing is moderate. A 24% return on equity is above the 17.5% return on total long-term capital because the loan costs less than the return it earns, which is favourable leverage.

Answer. Current 1.8; quick 1.2; GP 30%; NP 10%; stock turnover 5.6; collection 36.5 days; D/E 0.6; cover 7; ROE 24%; ROCE 17.5%.

How liquidity ratios react

Move the sliders to see why a business stuffed with unsold stock can look safe on the current ratio and weak on the quick ratio.

Adjust Current assets, of which stock, Current liabilities and see Current ratio, Quick ratio, Working capital change.

Check what you just learned

1. Current assets 6,00,000; current liabilities 3,00,000; stock 2,00,000. Quick ratio is
  • 1.33 (correct)
  • 2.0
  • 0.67
  • 3.0

(6,00,000 - 2,00,000) / 3,00,000 = 1.33.

2. COGS 9,00,000; average stock 1,50,000. Stock turnover is
  • 0.17 times
  • 9 times
  • 1.5 times
  • 6 times (correct)

9,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 6.

Common mistakes

  • Including prepaid expenses and stock in quick assets.
  • Using total sales instead of credit sales for debtors turnover when credit sales are given.
  • Quoting a ratio without saying what it means.
Exam tip

Write the formula, then the substitution, then the answer with its unit (times, days, % or ratio). Marks are given for each of the three.

Try it yourself: A firm's return on equity rose from 12% to 18% but its debt-equity ratio rose from 0.5 to 2.0. Is that good news?

Model answer. Not necessarily. Part or all of the rise may come from higher borrowing rather than better operations, and the firm is now much more exposed if profits fall. Look at ROCE and interest coverage to see whether operating performance improved.

topics.title: Cash flow statement
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain why cash flow differs from profit
  • Prepare a cash flow statement (indirect method) in three sections
  • Interpret the result

About 60 minutes

A profitable business can run out of cash, and a loss-making one can have plenty for a while. Profit is measured on the accrual basis; cash flow follows the money. The cash flow statement (required for most companies under AS 3 or Ind AS 7) explains how the cash balance changed during the year, in three sections.

Three sections
SectionIncludesExamples
Operating activitiesCash from the main businessNet profit adjusted for non-cash items and working capital changes
Investing activitiesBuying and selling long-term assets and investmentsPurchase of machinery, sale of equipment, interest received
Financing activitiesRaising and repaying capital and loansIssue of shares, loan repaid, dividend paid

In the indirect method, start with net profit before tax and adjust. Add back depreciation and other non-cash charges and losses on sale of assets, subtract gains on sale of assets. This gives operating profit before working capital changes. Then adjust for working capital: an increase in debtors or stock uses cash (subtract), a decrease releases cash (add); an increase in creditors provides cash (add), a decrease uses cash (subtract).

Tip

A fast test for each working capital line: if an asset goes up, cash goes down; if a liability goes up, cash goes up.

Worked example

Cash flow statement (indirect method)

Net profit before tax 2,00,000 (tax ignored). Depreciation 50,000; loss on sale of machinery 5,000. Debtors increased by 30,000; stock decreased by 20,000; creditors increased by 25,000. Machinery bought for 1,50,000; old machinery sold for 35,000. Shares issued 1,00,000; loan repaid 60,000; dividend paid 20,000. Opening cash 25,000. Prepare the cash flow statement.

  1. Operating profit before working capital changes = 2,00,000 + 50,000 + 5,000 = 2,55,000.
  2. Working capital: -30,000 (debtors up) + 20,000 (stock down) + 25,000 (creditors up) = +15,000. Cash from operating activities = 2,55,000 + 15,000 = 2,70,000.
  3. Investing: -1,50,000 (machinery bought) + 35,000 (machinery sold) = -1,15,000.
  4. Financing: +1,00,000 (shares) - 60,000 (loan) - 20,000 (dividend) = +20,000.
  5. Net increase in cash = 2,70,000 - 1,15,000 + 20,000 = 1,75,000.
  6. Closing cash = 25,000 + 1,75,000 = 2,00,000.

Answer. Operating +2,70,000; investing -1,15,000; financing +20,000; closing cash 2,00,000.

Check what you just learned

1. An increase in debtors during the year
  • Increases operating cash flow
  • Decreases operating cash flow (correct)
  • Is a financing item
  • Is an investing item

Cash is tied up in receivables.

2. Dividend paid is classified under
  • Financing (correct)
  • Operating
  • Investing
  • None

Dividend paid to owners is a financing outflow (for the company).

Common mistakes

  • Adding an increase in debtors instead of subtracting it.
  • Showing purchase of fixed assets in operating activities.
Exam tip

End every cash flow answer with 'Opening cash + net increase = closing cash' and tick it to the balance sheet figure. That one check catches most mistakes.

Try it yourself: Why is depreciation added back in the cash flow statement?

Model answer. Depreciation is deducted in arriving at net profit but no cash leaves the business. To arrive at cash from operations from a profit figure, such non-cash charges are added back.

topics.title: Published financial statements, standards and earnings quality
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Identify the components of a company's financial statements
  • Describe the role of Schedule III, Ind AS, IFRS and the auditor's report
  • Recognise warning signs of poor earnings quality

About 55 minutes

A company's annual report is the sole public record of its finances. Under the Companies Act, 2013 the financial statements consist of the balance sheet, the statement of profit and loss, the cash flow statement, the statement of changes in equity (where applicable) and notes, including a summary of significant accounting policies. Schedule III prescribes how items are classified and disclosed. Companies following Ind AS use Division II of Schedule III.

What you find in an annual report

  • Directors' report and management discussion
  • Standalone and consolidated financial statements
  • Notes to accounts: policies, contingent liabilities, related-party transactions
  • The auditor's report, which gives an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view
  • For listed companies, additional disclosures under SEBI's listing regulations

Ind AS are converged with IFRS issued by the International Accounting Standards Board. Convergence means Indian rules follow IFRS closely but with some carve-outs for the Indian context. The aim is comparability for global investors. Standards you will meet later include Ind AS 1 (presentation), Ind AS 2 (inventories), Ind AS 7 (cash flows), Ind AS 16 (property, plant and equipment) and Ind AS 115 (revenue from contracts with customers).

Earnings management means using judgment in the choice of accounting estimates and policies to shape reported profit, from mild smoothing to outright fraud. It is not always illegal, but it reduces the usefulness of the statements. Warning signs include profits growing while cash from operations lags, receivables growing much faster than sales, frequent changes in accounting policy, unusually large 'other income', and an auditor's qualification or emphasis of matter.

In India

The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) can investigate professional misconduct by auditors of larger companies. For listed companies, quarterly results are also filed with the stock exchanges, so analysts can test the trend every three months.

Worked example

A quick earnings-quality screen

A company's sales rose from 50 crore to 55 crore (one year). Receivables rose from 8 crore to 11.6 crore. Net profit rose from 4 crore to 6 crore. Cash flow from operations fell from 5 crore to 2 crore. What do the numbers suggest?

  1. Sales growth = (55 - 50)/50 = 10%.
  2. Receivables growth = (11.6 - 8)/8 = 45%, more than four times sales growth.
  3. Profit growth = (6 - 4)/4 = 50%.
  4. Cash flow from operations fell by 60%, while profit rose 50%.
  5. Interpretation: profits are being booked but not collected. Possible causes are aggressive revenue recognition, extended credit terms to push sales, or customer difficulty. The analyst should read the notes on revenue recognition and ageing of receivables, and the auditor's report, before relying on the profit figure.

Answer. Sales +10%, receivables +45%, profit +50%, operating cash -60%: a pattern worth investigating.

Check what you just learned

1. Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes
  • Rates of depreciation only
  • Format and disclosure of financial statements (correct)
  • Income tax rates
  • Audit fees

It sets out balance sheet and profit and loss formats.

2. Ind AS is converged with
  • US GAAP
  • UK GAAP
  • IFRS (correct)
  • None

Ind AS follows IFRS with limited carve-outs.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming that an unqualified audit opinion guarantees quality of earnings. It speaks to true and fair presentation, not to future performance.
  • Treating Ind AS and AS as the same.
Exam tip

When asked to comment on a set of statements, link at least two numbers and give a reason. 'Profit rose but cash fell, which could indicate...' scores more than listing percentages.

Try it yourself: List four warning signs of poor earnings quality.

Model answer. Profit rising while operating cash flow falls; receivables growing much faster than sales; frequent changes in accounting policies or estimates; large one-off other income; qualified audit opinion or emphasis of matter.

topics.title: Computerised accounting and GST in the books
topics.html:
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain how accounting software changes the work
  • Record purchases and sales with GST and compute net GST payable
  • Describe the controls needed in a computerised system

About 60 minutes

In accounting software such as Tally Prime, Zoho Books or a custom ERP, you enter a voucher (purchase, sale, receipt, payment, journal) and the software posts to the ledger and updates the trial balance and statements instantly. The logic is exactly the double entry you have just learned. What changes is speed, accuracy of posting and reporting. What does not change is the need to understand the entry. If you cannot say what should be debited and credited, you cannot tell when the software has been set up wrongly.

Controls that still matter

  • User access and role-based permissions
  • Regular backups and a tested restore
  • Audit trail (log of who changed what)
  • Bank reconciliation done monthly
  • Review of exception reports, for example negative stock or ledgers with unusual balances

Goods and Services Tax is a destination-based tax on supply. The supplier collects it from the buyer and passes it to the government after taking credit for the tax paid on purchases. A registered business is therefore only a collector: GST on sales (output tax) less GST on purchases (input tax credit) is the net amount paid. Within a state, the tax is split into CGST and SGST (UTGST in union territories). Between states, IGST is charged. Rates depend on the goods or service and change from time to time; the rate used below is illustrative.

Formula · Net GST payable

Output GST on sales - Input tax credit on purchases

A positive result is paid in cash; a negative result is carried forward as credit.

Watch out

Input GST is not an expense. Do not add it to the cost of purchases, except where credit is blocked or the business is not registered. Check the current rules at the official GST portal.

Worked example

Intrastate purchase and sale with GST at 18%

A registered trader buys goods worth 1,00,000 plus GST at 18% (9% CGST and 9% SGST) on credit from a supplier in the same state. He sells goods worth 1,50,000 plus 18% GST to a customer in the same state on credit. Pass the journal entries and compute GST payable.

  1. Purchase: Purchases Dr 1,00,000; Input CGST Dr 9,000; Input SGST Dr 9,000 / To Supplier 1,18,000.
  2. Sale: Customer Dr 1,77,000 / To Sales 1,50,000; To Output CGST 13,500; To Output SGST 13,500.
  3. Set-off: Output CGST Dr 13,500 / To Input CGST 9,000 and To CGST payable 4,500. Output SGST Dr 13,500 / To Input SGST 9,000 and To SGST payable 4,500.
  4. Net GST payable = 27,000 output - 18,000 input = 9,000 (CGST 4,500 + SGST 4,500).
Journal entries

Input SGST A/c Dr9,000

To CGST payable A/c4,500
set-off SGSTOutput SGST A/c Dr13,500To Input SGST A/c9,000

Answer. GST payable 9,000: CGST 4,500 and SGST 4,500.

What GST does to an invoice

Set the price before tax and the GST rate on the invoice. Intrastate, the tax splits equally into CGST and SGST.

Adjust Price before tax, GST rate and see Total GST, CGST (half), SGST (half), Invoice total change.

Check what you just learned

1. For a registered trader, input tax credit on purchases is
  • An expense
  • Added to the cost of goods
  • Ignored
  • Adjusted against output tax (correct)

It is set off against output tax.

2. On an interstate supply the tax charged is
  • CGST + SGST
  • UTGST only
  • IGST (correct)
  • None

Interstate supplies attract IGST.

Common mistakes

  • Adding input GST to purchases and then also claiming credit.
  • Treating GST payable as an expense in the profit and loss account.
Exam tip

Show Output GST, Input GST and Net payable in three lines. A clean layout wins marks even if the base amount is slightly off.

Try it yourself: Name three controls a small business should keep when moving to accounting software.

Model answer. Role-based user access, regular offsite backups with a tested restore, an audit trail of changes, monthly bank reconciliation and review of exception reports.

capstone.title: Final assessment and revision pack
capstone.summary: Revision sheets, practice numericals with full solutions, a software lab and a final test across all six units.
capstone.intro:
You now have the full toolkit. This last step has three parts: practise the numericals below, build the books in software, and take the final assessment of 48 questions covering every unit.

Formula sheet

  • Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital
  • Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit - Drawings + Additional capital
  • SLM depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life
  • WDV depreciation = Rate x Opening book value
  • COGS = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock
  • Gross profit = Net sales - COGS
  • Discount on a bill = Face value x Rate x Months / 12
  • Closing consignment stock = Unsold units x Cost + Consignor's expenses x Unsold / Sent
  • Subscription income = Received - Opening outstanding + Closing outstanding + Opening advance - Closing advance
  • Current ratio = CA / CL; Quick ratio = (CA - Stock - Prepaid) / CL
  • Debtors turnover = Net credit sales / Average debtors; Collection period = 365 / Turnover
  • Debt-equity = Debt / Equity; Interest coverage = EBIT / Interest
  • ROE = Net profit / Equity x 100; ROCE = EBIT / (Equity + Long-term debt) x 100
  • Net GST payable = Output GST - Input tax credit

The course on one page

  1. Accounting records, classifies and reports transactions so that users can decide.
  2. Every transaction has two equal effects; debits equal credits.
  3. Journal first, ledger second, trial balance third; BRS and rectification protect accuracy.
  4. Capital items go to the balance sheet, revenue items to the profit and loss account.
  5. Spread the cost of assets by depreciation; value stock at the lower of cost and NRV.
  6. Adjust for outstanding, prepaid, accrued and advance items so each year bears its own costs.
  7. Final accounts: trading account, profit and loss account, balance sheet. Net profit goes to capital.
  8. Non-profit organisations use receipts and payments, income and expenditure, and balance sheet; surplus goes to the general fund.
  9. Bills of exchange, consignment and joint venture are agency or credit arrangements with their own account formats.
  10. Analysis uses comparison, ratios and cash flow; profit is not cash.
  11. Accounting software and GST change the speed, not the logic.

How a typical university paper is set

70-mark external paper (pattern used by several universities such as Gurugram University).

  • 7 short-answer questions of 2 marks each, all compulsory (14 marks)
  • 8 questions of 14 marks each, 2 from each of 4 units; attempt 4, one from each unit (56 marks)
  • 30 marks for class tests, assignments, presentation and attendance

Patterns differ by university. Check your own question paper format and adapt.
steps: Lab 1: Create a company and ledgers. Create Rohan Stationers with 1 April 2026 as the start. Create ledgers: Cash, Capital, Furniture, Purchases, Sales, Rent, Gupta (sundry debtor), Verma & Co (sundry creditor). Expected: Eight ledgers with correct groups.

Lab 2: Enter the April vouchers. Enter the eight transactions of Worked Example WE2.1.1 as contra, journal, receipt, payment, sales and purchase vouchers. Expected: Cash balance 2,55,000 Dr. Gupta 15,000 Dr. Verma & Co 30,000 Cr.
Lab 3: Trial balance check. Display the trial balance at 30 April 2026. Expected: Debit and credit totals both 4,20,000, matching WE2.3.1.
Lab 4: Bank reconciliation in software. Add a bank ledger, enter the data of WE2.5.1 and use the reconciliation feature to reach 94,500. Expected: Pass book balance 94,500.

Lab 5: Depreciation schedule in a spreadsheet. Build a five-year SLM and WDV schedule for the machine in WE3.2.1 with a formula for each cell. Expected: SLM 90,000 a year; WDV 1,00,000, 80,000, 64,000, 51,200, 40,960.
Lab 6: GST voucher. Enable GST and enter the purchase and sale of WE6.5.1. Print the GST computation. Expected: Net GST payable 9,000 (CGST 4,500, SGST 4,500).

N1 10 marks · easy Pass journal entries for: (a) Started business with cash 2,00,000 and furniture 50,000. (b) Bought goods on credit from Hari 30,000. (c) Sold goods for cash 45,000. (d) Paid rent 6,000. (e) Paid Hari 20,000 in cash against his account of 30,000, and he allowed a discount of 1,000.
Show the solution
  1. (a) Cash Dr 2,00,000; Furniture Dr 50,000 / To Capital 2,50,000.
  2. (b) Purchases Dr 30,000 / To Hari 30,000.
  3. (c) Cash Dr 45,000 / To Sales 45,000.
  4. (d) Rent Dr 6,000 / To Cash 6,000.
  5. (e) Hari Dr 21,000 / To Cash 20,000 and To Discount received 1,000.

Answer. Five balanced entries; Hari's balance after entry (e) is 9,000.

N2 10 marks · medium The pass book shows a bank balance of 62,000 (credit). Cheques deposited 14,000 are not yet credited; cheques issued 9,000 are not yet presented; the bank credited interest 1,200 and debited an insurance premium 3,500, neither entered in the cash book. Find the cash book balance.
Show the solution
  1. Start with the pass book balance 62,000.
  2. Add cheques deposited but not yet credited: 62,000 + 14,000 = 76,000.
  3. Deduct cheques issued but not yet presented: 76,000 - 9,000 = 67,000. This is the correct adjusted cash book balance.
  4. The cash book before correction = 67,000 - 1,200 (interest not yet entered) + 3,500 (premium not yet entered) = 69,300.

Answer. Cash book balance before correction was 69,300 (debit).

N3 8 marks · medium Pass rectifying entries: (a) Credit sales of 7,000 to Rakesh were posted to Rajesh's account. (b) The purchases book was overcast by 2,000 and the difference was carried to a suspense account. (c) Machine repairs of 5,000 were debited to the Machinery account.
Show the solution
  1. (a) Rakesh Dr 7,000 / To Rajesh 7,000.
  2. (b) Overcast purchases means Purchases is debited 2,000 too much, so suspense was credited. Suspense Dr 2,000 / To Purchases 2,000.
  3. (c) Repairs Dr 5,000 / To Machinery 5,000.

Answer. Three rectifying entries; the suspense account closes after (b).

N4 10 marks · hard A machine costing 2,40,000 was bought on 1 July 2024. The firm charges depreciation at 10% on the written-down value and closes books on 31 March. The machine was sold on 1 October 2026 for 1,50,000. Calculate depreciation for each year and the profit or loss on sale.
Show the solution
  1. 2024-25: nine months (July to March). 2,40,000 x 10% x 9/12 = 18,000. Book value 2,22,000.
  2. 2025-26: full year on 2,22,000: 22,200. Book value 1,99,800.
  3. 2026-27 up to 1 October: six months: 1,99,800 x 10% x 6/12 = 9,990. Book value at sale = 1,89,810.
  4. Sale price 1,50,000, so loss on sale = 1,89,810 - 1,50,000 = 39,810.

Answer. Depreciation 18,000; 22,200; 9,990. Loss on sale 39,810.

N5 10 marks · medium Opening stock 200 units at 40. Purchases: 300 units at 44, then 500 units at 48. Sales during the period were 600 units. Find closing stock and cost of goods sold under (a) FIFO and (b) weighted average.
Show the solution
  1. Total units 1,000; total cost = 200 x 40 + 300 x 44 + 500 x 48 = 8,000 + 13,200 + 24,000 = 45,200. Closing units = 400.
  2. (a) FIFO: closing 400 units come from the last purchase at 48 = 19,200. COGS = 45,200 - 19,200 = 26,000.
  3. (b) Weighted average cost = 45,200 / 1,000 = 45.20. Closing stock = 400 x 45.20 = 18,080. COGS = 600 x 45.20 = 27,120.

Answer. FIFO: stock 19,200, COGS 26,000. Weighted average: stock 18,080, COGS 27,120.

N6 14 marks · medium Gross profit is 2,50,000. Salaries paid 60,000 (6,000 outstanding); rent paid 24,000 (4,000 prepaid); insurance paid 9,000 (1,500 unexpired); depreciation 20,000; bad debts 3,000; commission received 15,000 (3,000 accrued but not received). Debtors after writing off bad debts are 80,000; a provision of 5% is required and the old provision is 2,000. Find the net profit.
Show the solution
  1. Expenses: salaries 60,000 + 6,000 = 66,000; rent 24,000 - 4,000 = 20,000; insurance 9,000 - 1,500 = 7,500; depreciation 20,000; bad debts 3,000; additional provision = 5% x 80,000 - 2,000 = 2,000.
  2. Total expenses = 66,000 + 20,000 + 7,500 + 20,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = 1,18,500.
  3. Income: gross profit 2,50,000 + commission (15,000 + 3,000 = 18,000) = 2,68,000.
  4. Net profit = 2,68,000 - 1,18,500 = 1,49,500.

Answer. Net profit 1,49,500.

N7 8 marks · medium A club received subscriptions of 1,40,000 during the year. Subscriptions outstanding at the start were 12,000 and at the end 18,000. Subscriptions received in advance were 4,000 at the start and 7,000 at the end. Find the subscription income for the year.
Show the solution
  1. Start with receipts 1,40,000.
  2. Less opening outstanding 12,000 (belongs to the previous year): 1,28,000.
  3. Add closing outstanding 18,000 (earned this year, not yet received): 1,46,000.
  4. Add opening advance 4,000 (received last year for this year): 1,50,000.
  5. Less closing advance 7,000 (relates to next year): 1,43,000.

Answer. Subscription income 1,43,000.

N8 8 marks · easy A bill of 90,000 drawn on 1 January for three months and accepted was discounted on 1 February at 12% per annum. Find the discount and the cash received (ignore grace days).
Show the solution
  1. Period from discounting to due date = 2 months (1 February to 1 April).
  2. Discount = 90,000 x 12% x 2/12 = 1,800.
  3. Cash received = 90,000 - 1,800 = 88,200.

Answer. Discount 1,800; cash 88,200.

N9 12 marks · medium A consignor sent 500 units at cost 80 each; he paid freight 2,500. The consignee sold 400 units at 110 each, spent 1,500 on selling expenses and earns 10% commission on sales. Find the closing stock value and the profit on consignment.
Show the solution
  1. Goods sent = 500 x 80 = 40,000. Sales = 400 x 110 = 44,000. Commission = 4,400.
  2. Unsold units = 100. Value = 100 x 80 + 2,500 x 100/500 = 8,000 + 500 = 8,500.
  3. Debits: 40,000 + 2,500 + 1,500 + 4,400 = 48,400. Credits: 44,000 + 8,500 = 52,500.
  4. Profit = 52,500 - 48,400 = 4,100.

Answer. Closing stock 8,500; profit 4,100.

N10 10 marks · easy Current assets 3,60,000 (including stock 1,20,000); current liabilities 2,00,000; net credit sales 9,00,000; average debtors 90,000. Find the current ratio, quick ratio, debtors turnover and collection period.
Show the solution
  1. Current ratio = 3,60,000 / 2,00,000 = 1.8.
  2. Quick ratio = (3,60,000 - 1,20,000) / 2,00,000 = 1.2.
  3. Debtors turnover = 9,00,000 / 90,000 = 10 times.
  4. Collection period = 365 / 10 = 36.5 days.

Answer. 1.8; 1.2; 10 times; 36.5 days.

N11 10 marks · medium Net profit 1,00,000; depreciation 20,000; stock increased by 15,000; creditors increased by 10,000; equipment purchased 80,000; loan raised 50,000. Prepare a cash flow summary and find the net change in cash.
Show the solution
  1. Operating: 1,00,000 + 20,000 - 15,000 + 10,000 = 1,15,000.
  2. Investing: -80,000.
  3. Financing: +50,000.
  4. Net change in cash = 1,15,000 - 80,000 + 50,000 = 85,000.

Answer. Operating +1,15,000; investing -80,000; financing +50,000; net increase 85,000.

N12 8 marks · easy A registered trader buys goods for 2,00,000 and sells goods for 3,00,000. GST on both is 12% and all trade is within one state. Find the net GST payable and the split between CGST and SGST.
Show the solution
  1. Input GST = 2,00,000 x 12% = 24,000. Output GST = 3,00,000 x 12% = 36,000.
  2. Net payable = 36,000 - 24,000 = 12,000.
  3. Split equally: CGST 6,000 and SGST 6,000.

Answer. Net GST payable 12,000 (CGST 6,000 + SGST 6,000).

faqs.q: Is financial accounting hard for someone from a non-commerce background?
faqs.a: It is easier than it looks. Nearly everything follows from one rule: each transaction has equal debits and credits. If you can handle Class 10 arithmetic and practise 20 journal entries, you can pass the paper.

faqs.q: Which units are most important for university exams?
faqs.a: Units 2 to 4 carry most of the marks everywhere: journal and ledger, rectification and BRS, depreciation, and final accounts. Check your own syllabus before you skip a unit.
Not for the exam in most universities. For a job, yes. Learn the manual logic first. Use the lab exercises in this course to build the same books in software.

faqs.q: How is Ind AS different from the AS my syllabus mentions?
faqs.a: Ind AS are converged with IFRS and apply to listed companies and unlisted companies meeting the notified net-worth threshold. AS are the older Indian standards used by smaller companies. Exam questions at BBA level rarely test the differences in detail.

faqs.q: Why does my balance sheet not balance?
faqs.a: Check, in order: the trial balance totals, whether each adjustment was entered twice (profit and loss and balance sheet), whether net profit was added to capital and drawings subtracted, and whether closing stock appears in the balance sheet.

faqs.q: Is depreciation a source of funds?
faqs.a: No. Depreciation is a non-cash charge. It reduces reported profit, but cash is generated only by the business's operations.

faqs.q: Should I memorise formulas or understand them?
faqs.a: Understand the logic and memorise the formula sheet at the end of this course. Examiners award marks for method even when arithmetic slips.

faqs.q: Where can I check the official rules?
faqs.a: ICAI publishes the accounting standards, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs publishes the Companies Act and Ind AS rules, and the GST portal publishes GST law. Links are in the references section.
